confirmed.title: A freeze followed by a partial burst catch-up stops all segment sealing for the rest of the run, and the lost time is never recorded
confirmed.description: The timeline-discontinuity confirmation needs `lag >= lag0 - 0.5`. Here lag0 (drift_lag_at_start, set once at line 865) is the lag of the FIRST report that went over tolerance. After a stall, FFmpeg's first progress report comes when the first buffered packet arrives, so lag0 includes the whole frozen interval. If the camera then delivers its few buffered seconds in a burst before the absorbed jump, lag drops by more than 0.5 s but stays far above tolerance. From then on: drift_since_mono is never cleared (excess > tol at line 859), the discontinuity branch never fires (lag < lag0-0.5), and `if anchored and not drift_suspected` (line 476) holds every closed segment in `pending` until the run ends. That can be days, because the stream keeps advancing, so there is no stall. Slow camera drift (10-50 ppm) would take tens of hours to win back the 0.5 s+ margin.
confirmed.failure_scenario: I reproduced it by driving the real `_read_progress` with fake progress blocks (scratch script drift.py). Live stream at lag ~0.5 s. A 15 s network freeze at t=59 s. The camera had 3 s buffered, sends them in a burst, and FFmpeg absorbs the rest. Reports are (59.04 s at +15 s), then live (63.0 s ...). Result: drift_since stays set, lag=12.0, lag0=14.96, `lag>=lag0-0.5` is False indefinitely. Consequences: (1) no hourly segment is sealed, hashed, archived or retention-eligible while the run lasts; after ~91 min R-005 CRITICAL fires and a diagnostic report is made. (2) When the run finally ends, the held segments are sealed without drift.set_break and without timeline_break/shift, so the ~12 s of lost real time gets no gap row. Footage after the freeze is also timestamped up to 12 s early (the drift correction is rate-limited and flagged time_correction_limited).
confirmed.suggested_fix: Confirm 'not catching up' against the lowest lag seen since the drift started, not the first one. While drift is suspected, keep `lv.drift_lag_at_start = min(lv.drift_lag_at_start, lag)` in _read_progress, or simply require that excess stays > tol for timeline_drift_persist_s (drift_since is already cleared when it does not). measure_jump already gives the right shift (12 s in the example). Add a unit test with a burst catch-up after the freeze.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the logic, and I reproduced it.

How the code behaves (src/sentinel/recorder/supervisor.py):
- lv.drift_lag_at_start is written only once, at line 865. That happens on the first advancing progress report whose lag is more than tol (3.0 s) above the baseline.
- From then on, drift_since_mono is cleared only when excess <= tol (lines 859-862).
- The discontinuity branch (lines 497-498) needs lag >= lag0 - 0.5.
- Sealing only runs `if anchored and not drift_suspected` (line 476).
- Suppose lag drops by more than 0.5 s after the first over-tolerance report but stays more than 3 s above the baseline. None of the three conditions can change, so the run holds every closed segment for as long as it lasts.
- Nothing else releases them. The stall check needs out_time to stop advancing, and here it keeps advancing. The held segments are only sealed in the post-loop block (lines 576-577), which runs without drift.set_break and without timeline_break_stream_s/timeline_shift_s.
- The finaliser (finalizer.py:355-363) only writes a source_discontinuity_absorbed gap from those run columns, so no gap row is ever made.

What happens on the laptop:
- No segment is sealed, hashed, archived or eligible for retention until the run ends. Runs on a continuous camera can last days, unless a pause or motion idle ends them, or storage fills and ends the run at critical level.
- R-005 CRITICAL ("Video is arriving but recordings are not being saved") is raised. The agent can do nothing about it.
- The lost real time (about 9-12 s) ends up presented as continuous footage, and later footage in that run is timestamped early.
- No files are lost: they stay on the SSD and are sealed when the run ends.

What limits it (why this is not critical):
- In production config.py allows only RTSP (TCP transport by default). input_format=mpegts is limited to the simulator.
- FFmpeg's MPEG-TS discontinuity absorption does not apply to RTSP. A freeze usually shows up there as a forward RTP timestamp jump, which keeps the lag at the baseline.
- So the trigger needs an absorbed loss (camera timestamps that do not advance across the lost time) plus a catch-up that only partly recovers. The catch-up can be a burst that straddles the 1 s -stats_period report, or buffered data delivered slightly faster than real time over several seconds.
- The freeze must also be shorter than stall_timeout_s (15 s).
- That is uncommon but plausible with some cameras. When it happens it is deterministic and does not recover by itself.

Fix: release the "not catching up" condition once the catch-up stops.
- One way: while drift is suspected, keep `lv.drift_lag_at_start = min(lv.drift_lag_at_start, lag)` in _read_progress, at the elif at line 863: add an else branch that updates the minimum.
- Another way: fire when excess has stayed above tol for timeline_drift_persist_s, and lag has not fallen by more than 0.5 s over the last few seconds.
- measure_jump/lag - baseline already gives the right shift.
- Add a unit test with a partial burst catch-up.
verdict.evidence:
Code read:
- supervisor.py:466-479: pending segments are sealed only when anchored and not drift_suspected.
- supervisor.py:497-518: the discontinuity check needs `lag >= lag0 - 0.5`.
- supervisor.py:854-866: lag0 is set once, when drift starts; drift_since is cleared only when excess <= tol.
- supervisor.py:572-577: at run end, pending segments are sealed with no break or shift.
- finalizer.py:355-363: the gap row is made only from timeline_break_stream_s/timeline_shift_s.
- config.py:65,75-76: stall 15 s, tol 3 s, persist 5 s.
- ffmpeg_cmd.py:54: -stats_period 1.
- config.py:38,302-305: production allows RTSP only.

Reproduction script: <reviewer scratch folder>\sk_drift.py. It calls the real RecordingSupervisor._read_progress with a fake clock, a fake stdout, and the real RunTimebase and DriftTracker.
- Input: a live stream at lag 0.5 for 59 s; a freeze; a first report of out_time 59.04 at +12 s; then 62.5 and after that real-time advance for 200 s.
- Output:
  `drift_since 1071.5 lag 9.5 lag0 11.96 base 0.0 brk 59.0`
  `fires? False`
- drift_since stays set and the discontinuity condition never becomes true, so segments are held indefinitely and no break is recorded.

confirmed.title: A schedule that records only on listed dates stops the whole configuration from loading once the last date has passed, so the recorder and the archive copier both refuse to start
confirmed.description: _check_conflicts runs on every load_config (config.py:468). Its 'never records' rule compares against datetime.now(): it passes only while some non-pause date period has not ended yet (`d.end > today`, lines 252-254), and otherwise raises ScheduleError (259-261). load_config turns that into a ConfigError. So a configuration that was valid when it was written becomes invalid on its own once the calendar moves past the last record/motion date. Every process that calls load_config then fails at its next start: the recorder service (C-001), the archive copier (archive/__main__.py:72-83 returns 1), and the CLI/service commands in winsvc/__main__.py. Nothing changed on the machine, yet the archive copier is down, so Swap and Return to service stop working.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Technician sets [schedule] enabled=true, default='pause', with no weekly record/motion periods, plus [[schedule.dates]] record 2026-12-01 .. 2026-12-31 (a site recorded only on event dates). It loads fine in November. On 2027-01-02 the laptop reboots (Windows update, power loss). load_config raises '[schedule] never records', the recorder shows C-001, SentinelArchive exits with 'Configuration error', and the agent cannot swap a full drive. Reproduced: parse_schedule with that schedule passes for a future date and raises for a date in the past.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Never make whether a configuration loads depend on the current date. Run the 'never records' check (with the today filter) only when a schedule is saved (GUI/setup/CLI validation). At load time, accept the schedule and, if it no longer records, show a status warning (for example P-001 already says 'No time to resume recording is scheduled'). At minimum, never raise this from load_config in the archive copier.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this. parse_schedule (schedule.py:186-232) always calls _check_conflicts (231). When the schedule is enabled, the "never records" rule only skips the error if some non-pause date period has `d.end > datetime.now()` (252-254). If no weekly record or motion periods exist and default is "pause" (or pause covers the whole week), it raises ScheduleError (259-261). load_config/_build_config calls parse_schedule at config.py:468 on every load and turns ScheduleError into ConfigError (469-470). archive/__main__.py _load (72-77) prints "Configuration error" and _cmd_run returns 1 (81-83), so SentinelArchive will not start. The recorder and the CLI/service commands share the same load_config, so they fail the same way. Nothing else stops this: there is no load-time bypass and no separate save-time check. This is a regression introduced by the 2026-11-10 fix that added the `today` filter.

Severity: no recordings are lost by the recorder failing, because the schedule would have paused anyway. But the copier cannot start, so Swap and Return to service stop working, and segments recorded in the last date period that were not yet copied cannot be archived. Every Sentinel process reports a configuration error the agent did not cause and cannot fix without editing the schedule, on a machine nobody touched. That fits "copier wedged / agent stuck", so high. The trigger is narrow: it needs an enabled schedule with no weekly record or motion time that records only on listed dates. Fix: run the date-dependent "never records" check only when a schedule is saved (GUI settings_pages.py:789 / setup / CLI). At load time, accept the schedule and show a status warning such as P-001. The archive copier should never fail on this check.
verdict.evidence: Read schedule.py:186-261 (parse_schedule -> _check_conflicts, with `today = datetime.now()` at 252 and the raise at 259-261), config.py:466-471 (parse_schedule inside load-time config build, ScheduleError -> ConfigError), and archive/__main__.py:72-83 (ConfigError -> "Configuration error", return 1). Repro script <reviewer scratch folder>\repro_sched.py ran parse_schedule({"enabled":True,"default":"pause","dates":[{"action":"record","start":"YYYY-12-01","end":"YYYY-12-31"}]}, "UTC") with today = 2026-11-12. Output: "2026 ok" and "2025 ScheduleError [schedule] never records: add a period with action = "record", or set enabled = false". The same configuration loads or fails depending only on the current date.

confirmed.title: docs/10 laptop step 1 (one-bay dock: 'Swap archive drive first and take the drive in use out') now locks the second SSD out for good; copying stops and the agent is stuck
confirmed.description: With 0.3.12 every Swap puts the drive on the awaiting-return list (worker.py:1026, _set_awaiting). A drive on that list is never written again until it is returned to service, or until Cancel swap clears the whole list. docs/10 'On the laptop' step 1 tells the agent to use Swap to take the in-use SSD_2 out of a one-bay dock so that SSD_1 can come back from the office. SSD_2 has not been to the office, so the agent will never return it. When SSD_1 fills and SSD_2 goes back in, Sentinel does not copy to it. Status is ABSENT, alert A-001 says 'No archive drive is connected', and the message says 'press Cancel swap'. That button is hidden in this state (see the next finding). Recordings pile up on the laptop until A-004.
confirmed.failure_scenario: I ran this in the venv with a one-bay fake locator. SSD_1 copy, Swap, out. SSD_2 in, copy. Then, following docs/10 step 1: Swap SSD_2, out. SSD_1 in, Return to service (ok), copy, fill, Swap, out. SSD_2 in. Result: steps return 'absent' forever, state ABSENT, alerts ['A-001'], swap_under_way(recorder view) = False, and the message reads 'ARCHIVE_SSD2 was taken out with Swap archive drive, so Sentinel does not copy to it ... press Cancel swap'. This happens on every office cycle with the single-bay dock.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Do not treat every Swap as 'going to the office'. Options: (a) put a drive on the awaiting list only when it was full, or when the operator says it is going to the office (a separate 'Swap for office' choice); (b) otherwise change docs/10 step 1 to use a removal that does not set awaiting, and tell the agent to press Cancel swap afterwards. In any case, fix the hidden Cancel swap button (next finding), so an awaiting drive that is not at the office can always be released.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding. In the uncommitted 0.3.12 working tree, every Swap puts the drive on a persisted awaiting-return list. That happens in two places: _do_swap at worker.py:1026 and _swap_idle at worker.py:1049. The list is cleared in only two ways. Return to service removes the one drive being returned (worker.py:852, remove=True). Cancel swap, via resume() at worker.py:243, clears the whole list. While a drive is on the list, _select (worker.py:353-354) never uses it.

docs/10_OFFICE_TRANSFER.md:36 tells the agent to use Swap to take the drive in use out of the Sabrent dock so the returned SSD can go in. The Sabrent dock is the deployment's dock (requirement U2; docs/09 and docs/04 say one drive at a time in it). Following that step puts SSD_2 on the list even though it never went to the office. Returning SSD_1 clears only SSD_1. When SSD_1 fills and is swapped out, SSD_2 goes back in and is never chosen. _step then sets ST_ABSENT with the _awaiting_text message (worker.py:437-439), which says to press Cancel swap. Recordings pile up on the laptop until A-004.

Nothing rescues the agent:
(1) Cancel swap is hidden. drive_pages.py:297 shows it only when swap_under_way(arc) is true, which needs 'awaiting_return' in the view. The recorder's status view built in archive/status.py:219-221 copies only running, state, drive, message, backlog, drive_label, drives and removal. It drops awaiting_return, so the button stays hidden even though the message tells the agent to press it.
(2) That view does pass 'drives', which lists SSD_2 as 'Back from the office (return it to service)' (drive_pages.py:54, worker.py:1554-1556). This sends the agent toward Return to service on a drive the office never copied. Return to service would not refuse it, because SSD_2 was swapped and has no copies after the swap. Only the agent's false tick on 'office checked' stands between that and deleting the only archive copies.

With two separate USB drives the step is not needed, but the doc explicitly covers the Sabrent dock. This happens on every office cycle with that dock, so it is not an edge case.

Severity: high, not critical. The copier is effectively wedged and the agent is stuck with a misleading message and a hidden button. Recordings are not lost at once, but they pile up locally and the UI points toward a destructive action.

Fix:
- Do not put a drive on the awaiting list for every Swap. Only do it for a drive that is full or that the operator says is going to the office, or add a separate 'Swap for office' action.
- Alternatively, change docs/10 step 1, but there is no visible button to release the drive afterwards.
- Either way, add awaiting_return to the view in archive/status.py:219-221 so Cancel swap shows.
- Add a per-drive 'Use this drive again (not sent to the office)' action, because Cancel swap also clears the listing for a drive that really is at the office.
verdict.evidence:
Code traced in the 0.3.12 working tree (git diff shows worker.py +107, docs/10 +14, drive_pages.py changed):
- worker.py:1026 and :1049: self._set_awaiting(att.drive_id / key, label) runs on every swap.
- worker.py:939-959: _set_awaiting persists awaiting_return.json. drive_id=None clears all, remove=True clears one.
- worker.py:852: return to service calls _set_awaiting(drive_id, remove=True), for the returned drive only.
- worker.py:243: resume() (Cancel swap) calls _set_awaiting(None), which clears all.
- worker.py:354: usable = {k: t ... if k != self._swapped_drive and k not in self._awaiting}, so an awaiting drive is never selected.
- worker.py:437-439: if res == 'absent' and self._awaiting_present, it sets ST_ABSENT with _awaiting_text(). worker.py:974-980: that text ends 'To keep using it without an office copy, press Cancel swap.'

- drive_pages.py:60-64: swap_under_way needs state in SWAP_STATES, removal or awaiting_return. With state ABSENT and removal None it is False, so resume_btn.setVisible(False) at drive_pages.py:297.

- docs/10_OFFICE_TRANSFER.md:36: 'With the Sabrent dock: Swap archive drive first and take the drive in use out'.
- docs/09_BENCH_TEST.md:109 and docs/04:76-80: one archive drive at a time in the Sabrent dock. docs/00_REQUIREMENTS.md U2: the deployment uses the Sabrent dock.
I did not rerun the reporter's simulation. The conclusion rests on reading the code paths end to end.

confirmed.title: With two drives inserted, a drive the copier refuses blocks the other, good drive forever
confirmed.description: _select() always picks the lowest-key drive that is not full (room[0]). If _attach() refuses it (review-drive layout, write test failed, read-only or write-protected, cannot confirm it is a separate volume, review exports recorded), _refuse() returns False. The drive is not remembered as refused. Every later step selects the same drive again and returns 'unusable'. The second drive, which is fine, is never tried. Two-drive operation is the 0.3.10-0.3.11 owner request.
confirmed.failure_scenario: I reproduced this in the venv. Drives A and B are inserted, and the drive with the lower key has a 'Recordings' folder (or its write probe fails). worker.step() returns ['unusable'] x6, att=None, status UNUSABLE / A-005. Nothing is copied although B is usable. The backlog grows until A-004.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Keep a per-drive refusal set (cleared when that drive leaves the scan or after a while, like FULL_RECHECK_S). In _select, exclude refused drives from 'usable' and 'room', so the next candidate is attached. Report the refused drive in drives[] and in the message.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute it and couldn't. The finding is real.

1. Nothing upstream removes the problem drive. VolumeScanLocator.scan() (locator.py:123-164) puts every drive whose marker says role 'archive' and has a drive_uuid into scan.candidates. It does no layout check and no write check. The refusals happen later, inside worker._attach() (worker.py:527-561): same-volume clash or "cannot confirm it is a separate drive", a review-drive layout, review batches recorded in the ledger, or a failed write probe (read-only, write-protected or failing drive). root_present() returning False fails the same way, but without a message. _refuse() (520-525) only sets unusable_reason, writes an event and sets ST_UNUSABLE. Nothing remembers that the drive was refused.

2. _select() (331-379) has no refused set. When att is None it returns usable[room[0]], the lowest drive_key that is not full. It does this on every step. So the refused drive is chosen every time, _step() returns 'unusable' at line 449-450, and the second drive is never tried. Stickiness (line 367) helps only when the good drive was attached before the bad one appeared. Two cases hit the bug: start-up or service restart with both drives inserted, and roll-over after the attached drive fills (it is then in _full_drives, so room = [the bad drive]).

3. I reproduced it in a scratchpad test that reuses Env, Bays and make_drive from tests/unit/test_archive_two_drives.py. Two archive drives, A has the lower key and holds a 'Recordings' folder. The results:
   - step() x8 returns 'unusable' every time, att=None, state UNUSABLE, alert A-005, 0 rows in archive_copies.
   - The status drives[] shows BOTH drives as use='standby', so neither the window nor the agent can tell which drive is the bad one. The message is "The inserted drive cannot be used as an archive drive" (A-005: "Use a different archive drive"), which is ambiguous with two drives inserted.
   - 8 'archive_drive_unusable' warning events were written to the ledger in 8 steps: one per poll, without limit.

Severity: high rather than medium. The copier is wedged although a good drive is present. The backlog grows until A-004. The non-technical agent at the remote site gets a message that does not say which of the two drives to take out. A secondary effect is a ledger warning event on every poll. Recordings stay on the internal SSD, so nothing is lost straight away. That is why this is not critical.

Fix: keep a dict of refused drive_key -> (time, reason). Drop an entry when its drive is gone from the scan, or after a re-check interval like FULL_RECHECK_S. In _select, leave refused drives out of 'room' (and out of the "all full" fallback) so the next candidate gets attached. Also: report the refused drive in drives[] (e.g. use='refused' with its label) and name it in the message and the A-005 detail, and write the refusal event once per drive and reason instead of on every poll.
verdict.evidence:
Code read:
- worker.py:331-379 (_select: room = sorted(k for k in usable if k not in self._full_drives); return usable[room[0]]; there is no refused set)
- worker.py:441-450 (if not self._attach(target): return "unusable")
- worker.py:520-561 (_refuse sets only unusable_reason, an event and the status; the review layout, ledger review batches and write probe are all checked in _attach)
- locator.py:123-164 (only the role and drive_uuid decide whether a drive is a candidate)
- worker.py:1173-1195 (_roll_over detaches the full drive, after which the refused drive is room[0])

Reproduction: scratchpad test <reviewer scratch folder>/rep/test_rep_refuse.py. It uses the repo test harness, with (A.root/'Recordings').mkdir() on the lower-key drive. Output:
['unusable' x8] att=None state=UNUSABLE alerts=[A-005] message='The inserted drive cannot be used as an archive drive. Not yet archived: 0.2 h.'
copies 0
drives=[{'label':'ARCHIVE_B','use':'standby',...},{'label':'ARCHIVE_A','use':'standby',...}]
archive_drive_unusable events: 8

confirmed.title: Return to service accepts and wipes a drive that was just swapped but never left the laptop; afterwards it is still shown as 'ready to be taken out'
confirmed.description: _return_drive checks four things: the drive is not att, a swap event exists since the last return, nothing was copied after the swap, and the sizes match. It does not check whether the drive was physically removed after the swap. While _swapped_drive == drive_id, the drive has provably not been to the office. Yet the return goes ahead: copies are marked TRANSFERRED and their files deleted. Retention (if enabled) then treats those recordings as having left the laptop. _swapped_drive is left set, so the emptied drive is still excluded and the page keeps saying it is safe or ready to be taken out.
confirmed.failure_scenario: I reproduced this in the venv. Copy, then Swap (state REMOVE_MANUALLY, drive still inserted). A confused agent then runs Return to service on that drive. Result: 'ARCHIVE_A was returned to service: 3 file(s) ... deleted from the drive.' Afterwards state is REMOVE_MANUALLY and _swapped_drive is still set.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Refuse while drive_id == self._swapped_drive ('take the drive out and have the office copy it first'). Better still, require a presence session for that drive closed after the swap event: archive_drive_sessions.gone_utc later than the swap's ts_utc.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this. _return_drive (src/sentinel/archive/worker.py:797-866) refuses in only four cases: the drive is self.att (line 814), there is no swap event since the last return (817), copies were made after the swap (822-831), or files are missing or have the wrong size (832-845). Nothing compares drive_id with self._swapped_drive. Nothing else stops it either. _poll_return runs before _select (line 418) and takes its target from scan.candidates, and the swapped drive is still a candidate. The GUI's _return (gui/app/drive_pages.py:466-485) only checks that the row is class READY with role archive, and a swapped drive passes both.

It can happen on the real laptop. If the eject during Swap succeeds (state SAFE), the volume disappears and Return says "not connected", so that path is safe. If the eject fails (state REMOVE_MANUALLY, a normal outcome when a handle is open or a USB bridge refuses), the drive stays mounted with its letter and shows in the Drives list as "archive drive SSD_n".

The worst realistic case is the wrong-drive pick that the 0.3.12 safeguards (docs/10 line 54) are meant to stop. SSD_2 is swapped but still plugged in. SSD_1 comes back from the office and is plugged in. The agent selects SSD_2 and fills in SSD_1's transfer sheet. All four checks pass. SSD_2's verified copies are marked TRANSFERRED to an office copy that does not exist, and they are deleted from SSD_2. TRANSFERRED counts as archived, so they are never copied to an archive drive again. The only copy left is on the internal SSD. If retention is enabled (it is off by default, config.py:165), retention/manager.py:122 treats TRANSFERRED as having left the computer and can delete that last copy too, so the recordings would be lost. Afterwards _swapped_drive stays set, and the status still says "Ready to take out / Do not unplug yet" for a drive that is now empty. The audit log also holds a false "moved to the office" record.

The agent has to tick the box and enter office details, so operator error is involved. But that is exactly the mistake these refusals exist to catch, and while the swapped drive has been in the laptop the whole time, it provably has not been to the office.

Severity: high, not medium. Archive copies are deleted from the wrong drive and falsely recorded as at the office, and it becomes critical if retention is on.

One caveat for the suggested fix: _load_swapped (lines 915-933) reloads _swapped_drive from a file after a restart. A drive swapped, carried to the office while the laptop was off, and plugged back in before the archive service starts would still have _swapped_drive set, and a plain "refuse if drive_id == _swapped_drive" would block that legitimate return. A better fix is to refuse when drive_id == self._swapped_drive and this process has seen the drive continuously since the swap (it was not reloaded from the file). Alternatively, require a presence session for the drive in archive_drive_sessions that closed (gone_utc) after the swap's ts_utc, with a message such as "SSD_n has not been taken out since Swap; take it out and have the office copy it first. Nothing was deleted." In either case also clear _swapped_drive or refresh the status after a successful return.
verdict.evidence:
Code read: worker.py:797-866 (the return checks contain no _swapped_drive check), worker.py:331-355 (_select keeps the swapped drive out of usable but it stays in scan.candidates), worker.py:414-420 (_poll_return runs before _select), worker.py:915-933 (_load_swapped after a restart), drive_pages.py:466-485 (GUI return only checks class and role), retention/manager.py:116-122 (TRANSFERRED counts as off this computer), config.py:165 (retention off by default), docs/10_OFFICE_TRANSFER.md:54 (the refusals the docs promise).

Reproduction: a copy of the test_archive_return.py fixture plus one test, run from the scratchpad (<reviewer scratch folder>/rt/test_repro_swapret.py). Steps: 3 segments copied, request_swap, step until "swapped", then a return request with the drive still inserted. Output:
after swap: swapped REMOVE_MANUALLY drive_uuid:dff0... None
step: waiting_for_removal
RESULT {'ok': True, 'message': 'ARCHIVE_A was returned to service: 3 file(s) (0.0 GB) recorded as moved to Office archive drive 3 and deleted from the drive.', 'files': 3, ...}
states {'TRANSFERRED': 3} videos 0
after: REMOVE_MANUALLY drive_uuid:dff0...
drives [{'label': 'ARCHIVE_A', 'use': 'take_out', ...}] message: "Do not unplug the archive drive yet. Click the "Safely Remove Hardware" icon..."

confirmed.title: Known-good and restored camera credential copies get the config folder's ACL, so operators can read and decrypt them
confirmed.description: mark_known_good() copies the camera secret to '<secret>.good' with _copy_atomic (shutil.copy2 + os.replace), and restore_known_good() (line 185-186) copies it back over the live secret the same way. copy2 does not carry the DACL. The new file inherits the configuration folder's ACL, and install gives that folder Users:(OI)(CI)RX (winsvc/commands.py:304-307). I tried to refute this and could not. It is real, and part of it is worse than reported.

1. The credentials file sits in the configuration folder. Its default is C:\ProgramData\Sentinel\config\camera.secret (winsvc/__main__.py:368, launcher/setup.py:119). Install gives that folder SYSTEM/Administrators F, the service RX and Users RX, all inheritable (OI)(CI) (winsvc/commands.py:304-307). The remove_account_aces step keeps SID_USERS.

2. selfcheck._copy_atomic (selfcheck.py:141-144) does shutil.copy2 to "<dest>.partial" and then os.replace. CopyFile does not carry the DACL, so the .partial file takes the folder's inherited ACL. os.replace then moves that ACL onto the destination. The comment at line 143 is wrong for this folder.

3. Nothing re-protects the file afterwards. mark_known_good (line 154) is called from window.check_now (window.py:643) whenever an administrator's check passes. restore_known_good (line 186) is called from rollback_to_known_good (window.py:708). CameraPage.save_failed (settings_pages.py:350-353) does tmp.write_bytes then replace, which also gives an inherited ACL. install_check only looks at write access.

4. Worse than reported: the recorder checks the credentials file's DACL at startup. service.py:199-203 calls platform.secret_file_problems. Any grant to an account outside SYSTEM, Administrators, its own account and NT SERVICE\SentinelRecorder adds "camera credentials file is accessible by other accounts", and startup stops with C-001 and EXIT_CONFIG. So the restore paths do more than leak the password: they stop recording.

Scenario: the agent saves a new camera account (written private by write_protected_credentials), say with a typo. The 3-minute watch fails and the automatic rollback runs. restore_known_good sees that camera.secret.good differs from the live file and copies it over with copy2+replace. The live secret now carries Users:(I)(RX). restart_recorder runs, and the recorder refuses to start with a permissions message. The watch is over, so nothing else happens. The laptop stays off until someone re-enters the camera account on the Camera page. A failed config save after a credential change (save_failed) gives the same result.

The leak itself also holds. camera.secret.good is created readable by Users on every passing admin check. The DPAPI blob is machine-scope with a fixed, public entropy (dpapi.py:6-13, 75-95), so any local standard user can decrypt it and get the camera password.

Severity: I rate it high, not critical. The stop needs a rollback that involves a camera-account change, or a failed save after one, and re-entering the account fixes it. But in that case it stops recording on an unattended laptop, so it is close to critical.

Fix: never copy the secret with copy2. Write .good, the restored live file and the '.restore' temp with winacl.write_private_file plus the secret_file_acl_argv icacls step and remove_account_aces, the same as credstore.write_protected_credentials. Or copy the source file's DACL explicitly. Also add Users-free ACL checks for .good.

confirmed.title: One unreadable file on the archive drive wedges all archive copying forever (no A-006, A-007 'not running')
confirmed.description: In _archive_segment, any OSError from _archive_file that is neither 'drive removed' nor 'disk full' is re-raised (lines 1147-1150) to the run loop, which counts an error and retries the same step. Two places raise such an error persistently: the read-back of a file that already exists at the destination (lines 1281-1282: io.exists(dest) leads to _read_hash(dest)), and the read-back of a file just written (line 1294). An I/O error such as EIO or CRC from a bad sector on the SSD does exactly that. pending_segments() is oldest-first with limit=1, so every later step picks the same segment, finds dest present, fails the read again, and never reaches any other recording. Unlike VerifyMismatch, there is no attempt counter, no set-aside, no _skip and no add_problem. After 3 errors the worker raises A-007 'Archive copying is not running', which is wrong because it is running. Reproduced with a throwaway test: a FaultyIO whose read_back raises OSError(EIO) for the first .ts file. Over 10 steps: 10 OSErrors, 0 archive_copies, 0 archive_problems, and the other two segments were never copied.
confirmed.failure_scenario: The archive SSD develops one unreadable sector under a freshly copied .ts file. Every 60 s the copier retries that one file and fails. Nothing more is ever copied to that drive. The 'Not yet archived' backlog grows to A-004 after 24 h, and retention cannot free space because nothing new reaches a removed drive. The agent sees A-007 'Archive copying is not running ... contact support', and swapping in a fresh drive is the only way out. The damaged file is never recorded as a problem.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Treat a persistent non-drive OSError on a given segment/drive/kind like VerifyMismatch: count attempts per key, and after verify_attempts set the destination aside if possible, call add_problem(drive, 'verify_failed', ...) (A-006) and add the segment to _skip so later recordings keep flowing. Do not report A-007 for a worker that is alive and retrying; use a separate 'copy errors' wording.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and couldn't. In src/sentinel/archive/worker.py, _archive_segment (lines 1147-1150) passes any OSError that _drive_error does not handle back up to the run loop. _drive_error only handles two cases: the drive root is gone, or the disk is full. A read error on a drive that is still present is neither, so it is re-raised. Nothing turns it into VerifyMismatch or UnverifiableCopy. ArchiveIO.read_back (io.py:78) is a plain open_unbuffered, so the OSError comes straight through.

The run loop (lines 281-288) adds one to self.errors, waits (backing off to at most 60 s) and calls step() again. step() asks for pending_segments(limit=1), excluding only _skip and source_failed. The failing segment is in neither set, so the same oldest segment is picked every time. It still has no copy recorded, the file is still at dest, so io.exists(dest) leads to _read_hash(dest) at line 1282 and the same error again.

None of the escape routes apply. There is no attempt counter, nothing goes into _skip, add_problem is never called (so no A-006), and nothing is set aside. _skip is only cleared when the drive is detached. Swap still works, because step() checks _swap before it looks for pending work, so swapping the drive is the only way out.

After 3 errors, status.py:90 raises A-007, titled "Archive copying is not running", with the text "contact technical support". That is misleading: the worker is alive and retrying. The status message itself says "had a problem and will retry automatically", which contradicts the alert.

The scenario is realistic on the deployed laptop. An unreadable sector, or a USB bridge that keeps returning an error for one file, gives a persistent EIO or CRC error while the drive stays mounted. One damaged file is enough to stop all later copying to that drive. The backlog then grows until A-004 fires, and the damaged file is never recorded as a problem. Recordings stay on the internal SSD, so nothing is lost straight away. That is why this is high (copier wedged, agent misled into calling support) rather than critical.

Fix: catch the non-drive OSError per segment, drive and kind, like VerifyMismatch. Count attempts, and once verify_attempts is reached, try to set the file aside, call add_problem(drive_id, 'verify_failed', ...) and add the segment to _skip, so later recordings keep copying. Use separate wording for "copy errors, retrying" instead of A-007 "not running".
verdict.evidence: Code read: worker.py lines 1105-1162 (_archive_segment, _drive_error), 1246-1307 (_read_hash, _archive_file: line 1281 exists(dest) leads to line 1282 _read_hash, and line 1294 read-back after write), 264-288 (run loop: errors += 1, retry), 440-487 (step(): pending_segments(limit=1, exclude=_skip|source_failed)), 506-511 (_skip only cleared on detach), io.py:78 (read_back = open_unbuffered, nothing wrapped), status.py:90-91 (software_errors >= 3 gives A-007), alerts.py:117 (A-007 is titled 'Archive copying is not running'). Reproduction: a throwaway pytest outside the repo (in the scratchpad rep folder, file test_rep_eio.py). It uses tests/archive_helpers FaultyIO, overriding read_back to raise OSError(EIO) for the first .ts file, with 3 segments of 1 MiB and 10 steps, simulating the run loop's error counting and _report_error. Output: 'errors 10 claimed 0 problems 0', then "alerts ['A-007'] Archive copying had a problem and will retry automatically. Not yet archived: 0.2 h." confirmed.title: Janitor gap-record retry hijacks a later run's open gap, closes it with a negative duration, flags a false clock anomaly and drops the live outage
confirmed.description: The M9 fix makes the janitor resubmit GapJob for runs with gap_recorded=0. When the retried run A has footage, process_gap calls begin_gap(start=A's last end). If a LATER run B's gap is open at that moment, begin_gap does not open a gap for A. It bumps B's gap (attempts+1) and rewrites ended_run_id to A (db.py:918-926). process_gap then calls first_footage_after_run(A) and finds B's first footage, and close_gap closes B's gap at B's first footage start. _close_gap_in accepts this because B's rowid is greater than A's, which is now the gap's ended_run_id. That end is before the gap's own start (B's last segment end). The result is a negative duration and clock_anomaly=1. The camera is still down, but no gap is open any more. The A->B outage is never recorded either.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Reproduced with the real Ledger and Finalizer (scratch script gapretry.py). Run A ends at 01:00:00. Its GapJob fails ('database is locked' while the archive process holds the write lock). Run B records 01:00:35-01:01:10 and drops, so B's gap opens at 01:01:10. The janitor retries GapJob(A). Ledger result: gap {start 01:01:10, end 01:00:35, duration -35.0, ended_run 'A', clock_anomaly 1}, and open_gap() is None. The ongoing outage after B is missing from status and exports, and the tamper-evident log carries a false clock anomaly.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In process_gap for a late job, do not reuse a gap whose ended_run_id belongs to a later run. Instead insert a closed BETWEEN_RUNS gap for A, from A's last end to the first footage after A, or to the open gap's start if that is earlier, and leave the later open gap untouched. Alternatively, give begin_gap a parameter that forbids bumping an open row whose ended_run_id is newer than ended_run_id.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding, and I reproduced it with the real Ledger and Finalizer.process_gap.

How it happens:
1. A GapJob that raises is caught in Finalizer._run_job and only logged. The run keeps gap_recorded=0.
2. The janitor runs every 60 s (janitor_interval_s=60) and resubmits a GapJob for every run in runs_needing_gap(). Startup recovery (recovery.py:91) does the same.
3. If a later run B has recorded footage and dropped before that retry, B's own GapJob has already opened a BETWEEN_RUNS gap at B's last segment end.
4. The retried process_gap(A) calls begin_gap. begin_gap finds B's open gap. That gap is not a planned reason, so it falls into the bump branch (db.py:918-926). The bump rewrites ended_run_id to A and returns B's gap id.
5. first_footage_after_run(A, A_end) returns B's first segment, since its start is after A's end.
6. _close_gap_in passes the run-order guard, because B's rowid is greater than A's and A is now the gap's ended_run_id. It closes B's gap at B's first footage start, which is before the gap's own start. The duration is negative and clock_anomaly is set to 1.

Nothing else prevents this:
- B's first seal had no open gap to close, because A's gap was never written.
- When the camera recovers later (run C), C's seal finds no open gap, so the outage after B is never recorded.
- The A->B outage is never recorded either.

Trigger: process_gap(A) must fail. The likely cause is 'database is locked' after the 5 s busy_timeout while the archive process holds the write lock. Then another run must start, record and drop before the janitor's next pass, or the service must restart before it. A flapping USB camera makes the second part plausible. The first part, a failed gap write, is uncommon.

Impact:
- No footage is lost.
- The hash chain stays valid, because the bad rows are written through _chained.
- The gap ledger and exports carry a false clock anomaly and a negative-duration gap.
- Two outages are missing from the evidentiary record.
- While the camera stays down, open_gap() returns None.

Severity: this falls short of critical or high, because recordings are intact and nothing wedges. It is more than low, because evidence metadata is wrong and misleading. I rate it medium.

Fix: in process_gap, or in begin_gap through a flag, when the open gap's ended_run_id belongs to a run with a higher rowid than job.run_id, do not bump that gap. Insert a separate closed BETWEEN_RUNS gap for A instead, from A's last end to min(first footage after A, the open gap's start), and leave B's open gap untouched.

confirmed.title: Storage-critical after a schedule pause or motion standby keeps the open gap labelled as planned
confirmed.description: run_forever checks `storage.sample()` at the loop top and `continue`s before `_switch_gap(RESUMING_REASON, ...)` (line 170). If storage is critical when a planned period ends, the open 'scheduled_pause' / 'motion_idle' gap is never ended. The whole storage-full outage is recorded as planned. In motion mode the loop also returns to _wait_for_motion, which writes 'motion_record' audit events ('Motion detected: recording') while nothing records.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Schedule pause 20:00-06:00, retention off. Overnight, free space falls below critical_free_gb (e.g. Windows Update downloads). At 06:00 the pause ends, storage is critical, the loop waits in 10 s steps, and the gap stays 'scheduled_pause' until space is freed, possibly days later. Exports then say 'paused by the recording schedule (planned)' for a period when the recorder could not record. The status treats the gap as a pause (gap_is_pause) for outage length. This is the same class of bug as H3, by a path the H3 fix did not cover.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In the storage-critical branch, call `self._switch_gap(str(RunEndReason.STORAGE_CRITICAL), 'storage_critical')` (it only switches planned or resuming gaps). Or move the RESUMING switch above the storage check, so begin_gap/close_gap later attach the right reason.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute it, and a repro confirms it. In run_forever (supervisor.py:159-170), the loop checks `storage.sample()` at line 164 and, when storage is critical, waits and `continue`s at line 168. That happens before `_switch_gap(RESUMING_REASON, "recording_resumed")` at line 170. No run starts, so begin_gap is never called either, and begin_gap's backup split (db.py:905-917) needs a failed run before it does anything. Nothing else ends the planned gap. _pause_for_schedule (lines 369-393) and _wait_for_motion (lines 312-338) only switch the gap when the next state is another planned one. _reconcile_gap_at_start only runs once, at startup.

Result: the open 'scheduled_pause' or 'motion_idle' gap stays open while storage is critical. Once space is freed, line 170 switches the gap to 'resuming' at that moment. So the planned gap is closed at the time space was freed, not when the schedule period ended. Exports (manifest.py) then describe the whole storage-full outage as a planned schedule pause. service.py:684-690 (gap_is_pause) also leaves that time out of the outage duration and the outage start time in status.

In motion mode the reviewer's extra point also holds. After motion, _wait_for_motion writes the audit event "Motion detected: recording", then the loop hits the storage-critical branch and nothing records. When keep_recording_s runs out, it writes "No motion: recording stopped" again. These are misleading audit events.

Why medium and not higher: no footage is lost or corrupted, and the hash chain is unaffected. The storage-critical condition still shows through the storage monitor and the status alerts, so the agent still gets told that storage is full. The harm is a wrong reason on the evidence record, plus the outage left out of status. Exports are evidence, so this matters, but it is not data loss.

How likely it is: storage has to cross the critical threshold during a pause, or between a motion-idle run ending and the next motion. That is possible but not common: a nearly full spool with retention off, a final segment written, or other disk use such as Windows Update.

The suggested fix is right. In the storage-critical branch, call `self._switch_gap(str(RunEndReason.STORAGE_CRITICAL), "storage_critical")`. switch_open_gap only switches planned gaps by default, so an open unplanned gap is left alone. Alternatively, move the RESUMING switch above the storage check: begin_gap then gives the 'resuming' gap its real reason on the first failure. But no run starts here, so the gap would stay 'resuming'. The direct STORAGE_CRITICAL switch is the better fix. Ideally, also skip the 'motion_record' audit event, or make it say storage is full, when storage is critical.

confirmed.title: W-002 and an escalated R-003 'Camera connection lost' stay CRITICAL all night after the camera recovers in a motion period
confirmed.description: motion_record_failures goes up for every run started while the mode is 'motion' that gets no media. This includes fail-safe runs started only because the detector was unhealthy, when no motion was detected at all. The counter is reset only by a later run with media (line 191-192). If the motion detector reconnects first after a camera outage (healthy, no motion), the supervisor goes back to _wait_for_motion and never starts another run. In status.evaluate, `motion_record_failures` then skips P-003 (line 134) and falls through to the outage branch. The outage is measured from resumed_mono (the fail-safe start), so it escalates. Partly overlaps the 2026-11-12 'camera offline during a motion period' finding; the persistence after recovery is the extra part.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Motion period at night. The camera reboots, so the detector becomes unhealthy and fail-safe runs end with connect_timeout; failures=3. The camera comes back, the detector gets frames first, and there is no motion. Until the next motion event (possibly morning) the status shows W-002 CRITICAL 'Motion was detected but could not be recorded' plus R-003 CRITICAL 'Recording stopped... Camera connection lost. Automatic recovery unsuccessful. Contact technical support', with overall INTERRUPTED. The camera is fine and the system is correctly waiting for motion. The non-technical agent is told to call support, and a diagnostic report is made.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Count a failure only when the run was started because motion was actually seen (snapshot seconds_since_motion <= keep_recording_s), not for fail-safe or schedule-change starts. Also clear (or stop escalating) the count when the supervisor enters motion standby with a healthy detector after the outage, or when the main stream is proven reachable. Then raise R-00x for the fail-safe outage instead of W-002.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this. The code path holds from start to end.

1. supervisor.py:171 sets `for_motion = self._mode_now() == "motion"`. That checks only the schedule mode, not why the run started. Lines 190-194 add 1 to motion_record_failures for every run with no media that does not end in GRACEFUL_STOP. Only a later run that gets media (line 191-192) sets it back to 0.

2. While the camera is down, the detector is unhealthy and not warming up. recording_wanted() (motion.py:214-221) then returns True through the fail-safe, so runs start and end in CONNECT_TIMEOUT with 0 media, and the counter climbs.

3. When the camera comes back, there are two likely races, and both leave the counter above 0:
   (a) The detector gets frames while the recorder is in backoff (up to backoff_max_s = 30 s). The next loop top gets MOTION_IDLE from _pause_reason(), and _wait_for_motion() is entered without resetting the counter.
   (b) The detector gets its first frame while a fail-safe run is still connecting. The in-run check at supervisor.py:529 ends that run with MOTION_IDLE before any media, which adds 1 more (MOTION_IDLE is not GRACEFUL_STOP).

4. _wait_for_motion() sets motion_idle=True but neither clears motion_record_failures nor resets resumed_mono. resumed_mono is still the time the first fail-safe run started.

5. status.evaluate adds W-002 CRITICAL whenever the counter is above 0 (status.py:116-117). P-003 is skipped because of `not m.motion_record_failures` (line 134), and scheduled_pause is False. confirmed.title: Motion is never confirmed when the second stream delivers fewer frames than analysis_fps: the fps filter's duplicate frames reset the min_frames count
confirmed.description: With stream_path set, the detector uses `-vf fps=<analysis_fps>,...`. FFmpeg's fps filter makes a constant frame rate by DUPLICATING frames when the source is slower, or when frames are missing from its timestamps. A duplicate is byte-identical to the frame before it, so MotionAnalyzer.feed scores 0 % and resets `_run` to 0 (lines 156-160). With min_frames >= 2 (default 2), every second analysed frame is a duplicate, so the count never reaches min_frames and motion is never confirmed. The detector still counts as healthy because frames keep arriving, so the W-001 fail-safe never fires either. The code already knows this risk for the key-frame path (comment at 124-126, `-fps_mode passthrough`) but not for the second-stream path. Nothing checks that the camera's second-stream frame rate is >= analysis_fps.
confirmed.failure_scenario: The camera's second stream is set to 2 fps (common for bandwidth) or drops frames under load; analysis_fps = 4 (default), min_frames = 2. Each source frame reaches the analyzer twice (A, A, B, B, ...): the pairs score 0, X, 0, X, so the count goes 0, 1, 0, 1. In 'motion' periods (nights/weekends) someone walks through and nothing is recorded, with no alert. Reproduced with MotionAnalyzer: the same moving frames confirm motion without duplicates and never confirm when each frame is doubled.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In MotionAnalyzer.feed, ignore a frame that is identical to the previous one (`if frame == prev: return self._run >= min_frames`, without resetting the count or replacing prev). Or drop the fps filter and pace without duplicating (for example `-fps_mode vfr` with `-r`, or `mpdecimate`). Also document or check that the second stream's fps should be >= analysis_fps.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute it. When stream_path is set, detector_argv (src/sentinel/motion.py:120-121) puts `fps=<analysis_fps>` at the front of the filter chain. Unlike the key-frame path (lines 123-126), it does not use `-fps_mode passthrough`, and nothing dedupes frames. FFmpeg's fps filter fills a slow source by repeating frames. A repeated frame is byte-identical to the one before it, so MotionAnalyzer.feed (lines 151-160) scores it 0 and resets _run to 0. With min_frames=2 and a source at or below analysis_fps/2, the count goes 0,1,0,1 and never reaches 2. Frames keep arriving, so healthy() stays true, the W-001 fail-safe never fires, and recording_wanted() stays false through real motion.

I checked this with the real FFmpeg 9.0.1 and Sentinel's own detector_argv and MotionAnalyzer, using a moving test pattern for 10 s:
- 2 fps source: half the frames are duplicates and motion is never confirmed.
- 3 fps source: a quarter are duplicates and only 18 of 40 frames confirm.
- 4 or 15 fps source: no duplicates, 38 of 40 confirm.

The failure gets worse as the source rate falls toward analysis_fps/2, or as min_frames rises (for example 3 fps against 4 with min_frames=4). The GUI allows analysis_fps up to 15, so a 7 fps second stream with analysis_fps=15 fails the same way.

Three things limit the impact, and they are why I rate it medium rather than critical:
1. The second-stream path is opt-in. The shipped config has stream_path = "", which uses key frames with passthrough and is not affected.
2. Common second streams run at 10-25 fps, well above the default analysis_fps of 4.
3. The documented on-site tuning step (`Sentinel.exe motion-test`, walking through the scene) would show MOTION never appearing, so a technician who follows it would catch the problem.

Still, nothing in the code warns about the setup, and at runtime the miss is silent: in motion-scheduled hours, real motion is not recorded and nothing alerts. The suggested fix is correct and small. In feed(), treat a frame equal to the previous one as "no new information": return the current state without resetting _run or replacing _prev. Alternatively, pace the stream without duplicating frames (for example `-fps_mode vfr`).

I read src/sentinel/motion.py lines 105-160. The fps filter is added only on the stream_path branch (line 121) and passthrough only on the key-frame branch (line 126). In feed(), a score of 0 resets _run (lines 156-159).

3 40 dups 10 confirmed 18
4 40 dups 0 confirmed 38
15 40 dups 0 confirmed 38

LiveView._tick (gui/app/liveview.py:105-131) shows 'No picture from the camera' only when state is no_picture AND there is no frame. Otherwise it keeps the old pixmap and computes the picture's age from taken_utc. That age is less than STALE_S (6 s) right after each state write, so the caption reads 'Live · <now> · about 5 pictures a second'. It alternates with a 'not updating' caption that names the wrong time. This breaks the module's own promise that a frozen picture can never be mistaken for a live one.

The preview FFmpeg ends after its 10 s I/O timeout, and the worker writes state 'starting' (old frame, taken_utc = now), then 'no_picture' (same) after each failed reconnect (backoff 2-15 s). The window keeps showing the last picture and repeatedly says 'Live · 14:03:12 ...' with an advancing time. The agent concludes that the camera is fine.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Store the frame's own time in _publish (for example self.frame_utc) and write that as taken_utc; write the state-change time in a separate field. When _run_ffmpeg ends or fails, clear `frame` (or have the window treat any state other than 'live' as 'no current picture' and show the no-picture or connecting text).

I could not refute this. PreviewWorker._write_state (src/sentinel/preview.py:245) always sets taken_utc to iso_utc(self.clock()), the time the state was written, not the time the frame was captured. Nothing clears self.frame when FFmpeg ends; only _clear() does that, and it runs only once the viewer's request has gone stale or on stop(). After a live session, the camera drops and FFmpeg exits on its 10 s I/O timeout. _run_ffmpeg then returns got=True, and _loop goes round at once: it writes state 'starting' with the old frame and taken_utc=now. The reconnect attempt fails, so it writes 'no_picture' with the same frame and taken_utc=now. The backoff then grows 2/4/8/15 s, and each later cycle writes both states again.

confirmed.title: An entry whose hash is valid but whose kind, table or value is a JSON list or object crashes verify_ledger, so V-003 is never raised and an examiner gets a traceback
confirmed.description: chain_pass treats an entry as well-formed when make_record(rec[...]) re-creates its text exactly (lines 991-997). make_record only formats the fields. For a non-string kind/table/key it falls back to canonical_json, so a record with "kind":["event"] or "table":{} round-trips and counts as well-formed. kind_rules then runs outside any try block: `kind not in VALID_KINDS` (line 1039) and `table in COVERED` (line 1068) raise TypeError (unhashable). Other spots crash the same way: `(a, b) in transitions.get(...)` in illegal_changes (line 688) when an archive_copies, archive_problems, archive_drive_sessions or retention_deletions entry holds a list or dict value, and `sum(pre.values())` / `any(pre.values())` on a genesis entry whose pre_existing_rows is not a dict of ints (lines 1050-1051). verify_ledger has no handler, so the whole report is lost, including the anchor_mismatch / record_altered findings already collected for earlier entries. The chain has no key, so anyone who can edit the database can recompute the hash of such an entry: this is a way to switch off tamper detection, not only to fool it.

The worker loop logs 'integrity worker error'. chain_report keeps its last value (None after a restart), so status shows last_check_ok null / true and V-003 never appears. Only a 10-minute generic verify_problem follows each crash. `Sentinel ledger verify --anchors-from <drive>` prints a Python traceback instead of 'RESULT: ALTERED', even when an earlier anchor would have caught a history rewrite.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In chain_pass, make well-formedness check the types: v == 1 (int, not bool), seq int, utc str, kind str, table str or None, key str or None, data dict or None. Anything else is entry_unreadable (and the chain is broken). Also wrap kind_rules and each check_key iteration in try/except (TypeError, ValueError, AttributeError, KeyError) and turn an exception into an 'illegal_entry' finding at that seq. Then a malformed entry is always reported as alteration, never a crash. Add a regression test with list/dict kind, table and state values.

I tried to refute this and could not; I reproduced it. In chain_pass (ledgerchain.py:991-997), an entry counts as well-formed when rec.get("v") == CHAIN_FORMAT and make_record(...) rebuilds the stored text exactly. make_record's s() helper (line 284) sends any value that is not a str to canonical_json, so "kind":["event"] or "table":{} round-trips and passes. The hash and link checks also pass, because the chain has no key and the attacker recomputes entry_hash. kind_rules (line 1022 -> 1039) then runs outside the try block. `kind not in VALID_KINDS` with a list, or `table in COVERED` with a dict, raises TypeError, and nothing in _Verifier.run or verify_ledger catches it.

- IntegrityWorker._loop (integrity.py:93-112) logs 'integrity worker error' and appends to recent_errors. chain_report is never assigned, so chain_altered stays False (None after a restart) and V-003 is never raised. The only sign is a generic verify_problem for 600 s after each hourly crash.
- diagnostics.py:124-130 catches the exception and writes 'could not be checked (...)' instead of ALTERED.
- The `ledger verify` CLI (ledgerchain.py:1246) has no handler and prints a traceback.

The impact goes beyond a fully recomputed chain, which is a documented limitation that saved anchors catch. Appending one such entry hides earlier anchor_mismatch findings, and stops the key_pass checks (record_altered and the rest) from running at all, so an anchored rewrite goes unreported.

I did not test archive_copies or archive_problems entries. My pre_rows variant built no forged entry, so it neither confirms nor rules out that spot. The kind and table crashes alone prove the finding.
2. It needs deliberate tampering by someone who can write to sentinel.db, most simply while the service is stopped. A running recorder would collide with the forged seq on its next append, which may raise its own discrepancy or failure signal.
3. No recording is lost or corrupted, and the recorder and copier keep running.

confirmed.title: A swap pressed while the drive is refused stays armed and prepares the next good drive inserted, putting it on the awaiting-return list
confirmed.description: request_swap() sets _swap. In _step the swap is handled only after a successful _attach. When _attach fails ('unusable'), _swap stays set with no expiry: _swap_deadline only limits a copy in flight. _no_drive() clears it only on a scan with no archive drive at all. So the next drive that attaches is swapped at once, even hours later. It is ejected or shown as 'take out', added to awaiting_return.json, and never written. Meanwhile 'archive swap' times out after 600 s with 'not ready to be removed ... contact technical support'.
confirmed.failure_scenario: I reproduced this in the venv. A (refused) and B are inserted. The agent presses Swap to get rid of the unusable drive, and step() returns 'unusable'. The agent pulls A. On the next step B attaches and _do_swap runs: the result is 'swapped', state REMOVE_MANUALLY, _swapped_drive = B, awaiting = [B], then 'waiting_for_removal' on every later step. Copying stops, and the agent is told to take out the good drive. The same happens with one bay if the refused drive is replaced by another within one poll.
confirmed.suggested_fix: When _attach fails while _swap is set, clear the swap: nothing that the request was about can be prepared, and _set explains why. More generally, tie a swap request to the drive that was attached when it was read (record drive_id), and drop it if a different drive attaches.

A drive taken out this way can never be returned to service. The refusal text ('was not taken out with Swap archive drive... Select the drive that came back from the office') points the agent at a different drive and does not give the real way forward (insert it, Swap, have the office copy it again). confirmed.suggested_fix: When eject (drives eject / Safely remove...) is run on a drive whose marker has role=archive, record the same 'archive_swap_ready' audit event (drive_id = 'drive_uuid:<uuid>', last_copy_id = max copy_id on that drive) before ejecting, or refuse with 'Use Swap archive drive'. Also change the refusal text to say what to do (insert the drive, press Swap, re-copy at the office).

Those roles are OS, software, recordings spool, ledger and logs (src/sentinel/drives/protected.py:76-89). Archive drives are not among them.
2. Neither eject path tells the copier or writes an event. The CLI path (src/sentinel/drives/cli.py:290-305) and the GUI path (_eject, src/sentinel/gui/app/drive_pages.py:512-521) do nothing except eject. The 'archive_swap_ready' event is written only in worker._do_swap (worker.py:1033) and worker._swap_idle (worker.py:1054).
3. The new uncommitted check refuses such a drive. worker._return_drive (worker.py:813-820) refuses any drive without a swap event since its last return, using ArchiveLedger.last_swap_since_return (src/sentinel/archive/ledger.py:305-318). tests/unit/test_archive_return.py:209-221 (test_the_drive_in_use_or_one_never_taken_out_is_not_returned) asserts exactly this refusal.
4. Sentinel itself recommends this route. COPIER_NOT_RUNNING (src/sentinel/archive/status.py:125-129) says "select it in the list and press Safely remove…". It is shown by the GUI Swap handler (drive_pages.py:344-346) and by `archive swap` (archive/__main__.py:107, 132). docs/04 line 97 says the same.
5. The refusal text sends the agent the wrong way. It tells them to "Select the drive that came back from the office" when they already did. If the copier is running when the drive is plugged back in, the drive is not in the waiting-for-return list. The copier re-attaches it, and Return then fails on the earlier check at worker.py:814 with "is the archive drive Sentinel is copying to now, so it has not been to the office". - Nothing is lost or deleted. Return refuses safely and the recordings stay on the drive and the laptop.
- The copier and recorder are not wedged.
- A recovery exists, as long as the drive is not stuck: plug it in, press Swap, have the office copy it again into a new folder, then Return. docs/10 "At the office" step 1 describes that recovery.
- The agent is not told any of this by the refusal, and the status text that sends them to Safely remove contradicts docs/10 step 1. So it is a misleading message with a workaround that costs an extra office trip.
- The A-007 scenario needs the copier to be down. Return itself also needs the copier running, so the drive cannot be returned until A-007 clears anyway.
- An earlier finding today (docs/REVIEW-2026-11-12.md, drives, eject.py:171, rated low) already noted that Safely remove ignores the copier. This finding is the new consequence created by the 0.3.12 swap-required check together with the Safely remove advice.

- Make `drives eject` refuse a drive whose marker says role=archive ("Use Swap archive drive"). Recording a swap event there is the other option, but it is weaker: the copier was not involved, so the index on the drive may be stale.
- Reword the refusals at worker.py:814-820 to give the way forward: plug the drive in, press Swap archive drive, and have the office copy it again into a new folder.

When Get-Disk reports an empty serial and WMI has one, the helper sees '' and throws IDENTITY_MISMATCH serial before anything is erased. That is safe, but the operator is told the drive changed, which it did not, and the drive can never be set up.

The agent types its last 4 characters and approves. The helper exits 3 and the GUI says 'The drive changed after it was confirmed. Nothing was erased.' This happens on every retry.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Use the same source on both sides. Either embed the fallback flag and have the helper read Get-CimInstance Win32_DiskDrive -Filter "Index=$($d.Number)" when Get-Disk's serial is empty (with the same normalisation), or do not use the WMI fallback for identity, only for display.

There is no Win32_DiskDrive fallback on the helper side, so it compares '' with the WMI serial and throws 'IDENTITY_MISMATCH serial' (exit 3).

The Python TOCTOU re-check (prepare.py:272-275) uses the same parser on both sides, so its fingerprints agree. _assert_plannable only needs has_hardware_identity, which a WMI-only serial satisfies. The run then reaches the helper at the 'verify' step (non-destructive) and fails. prepare.py:299-300 reports this as "The drive changed after it was confirmed. Nothing was erased." The scenario is realistic: some USB/UASP bridges leave MSFT_Disk.SerialNumber blank while Win32_DiskDrive reports one, and the code's own fallback exists for exactly that case. The workaround is to use a different drive or enclosure. Medium severity: no data loss and the recorder is not wedged, but the agent is blocked with a misleading message. Either pass a flag so the helper reads Win32_DiskDrive (Index = disk number, normalised the same way) when Get-Disk's serial is empty, or use the WMI serial only for display and keep the Get-Disk serial for identity.

confirmed.title: Safely remove is bound only to a disk number from a possibly old list, and its 'gone' check matches lookalike hardware
confirmed.description: The GUI passes only '--disk N' (drive_pages.py:519). cmd_eject finds whatever disk now has that number. Unlike prepare, there is no --fingerprint or expected identity. Disk numbers are reused when drives are plugged in and out, so the wrong drive (for example the archive drive in use) can be ejected. After a successful eject, verify_gone looks for any disk with the same hardware_key. Behind docks or bridges that report placeholder serials, a second disk of the same model and size has the same key, so success is reported as 'The drive did not disconnect. Do not unplug it. Contact technical support.'
confirmed.failure_scenario: Two identical SSDs report serial 000000000000000000 in separate enclosures. The agent ejects SSD_1. Windows removes it, but the loop still finds SSD_2 with the same hardware_key for 15 s and shows 'did not disconnect. Do not unplug it. Contact technical support.' The agent is stuck with a drive that is in fact safe to remove.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Pass the fingerprint shown (and drive_uuid if any) from the GUI to 'drives eject' and refuse if it changed. In verify_gone, check that the specific PnP device ID / device path (or the volume GUIDs) is gone instead of the hardware_key.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the main part of this finding, the false "did not disconnect" message after a safe removal that worked. I reproduced it with a mocked device tree.

verify_gone (src/sentinel/drives/eject.py:169-171) treats the drive as still connected while any listed disk satisfies identity.same_device(ident). same_device compares hardware_key only: (serial, unique_id, model, size_bytes, bus_type) (src/sentinel/drives/model.py:233, 247). Nothing on this path filters out placeholder serials or placeholder UniqueIds. The raw UniqueId from Get-Disk goes straight into the key (windows_enum.py:186). Two disks of the same model and size, in separate enclosures whose bridges both fill in placeholder serials and the same filler UniqueId, therefore have equal keys. The shared_device check (eject.py:149-159) does not stop this, because separate enclosures have separate removable device nodes. So the eject goes ahead and succeeds. The other disk is still listed, the loop runs for 15 s, and it returns "The drive did not disconnect. Do not unplug it. Contact technical support." The drive has in fact been removed safely, and the agent is told not to unplug it. The docs record that a filler UniqueId (5000000000000001) and placeholder serials (eighteen zeros) do occur on real bridges (docs/04 lines 129-145).

Why medium and not high: the hardware documented for this deployment probably does not trigger it. The Samsung T7 reports a real serial, so two T7s have different keys. The Sabrent EC-HD2B dock, which reports placeholder serials, is refused earlier as shared_device. So the bug needs a pair of lookalike single-bay enclosures, which is plausible but not the documented setup. When it does happen, the agent is stuck with a wrong message, and there is a workaround: the drive has already disappeared from the Drives list.

The secondary claim, that eject is bound to a possibly stale disk number, is technically true. cmd_eject (cli.py:290-296) looks up whatever disk now has that number. Unlike prepare, it takes no fingerprint. The impact is small, though. An eject erases nothing, and protected disks and disks holding the system, boot volume or page file are refused (eject.py:137). If the copier has the archive drive's files open, Windows vetoes the eject. At worst a wrong drive is ejected and can be plugged back in. That part alone would be low.

Fix:
- In verify_gone, check that the target's specific PnP instance (disk.pnp_device_id) no longer appears. Alternatives are to check that CM_Locate_DevNodeW on it fails, or to compare device_path / volume GUIDs, instead of comparing hardware_key.
- Have the GUI pass the shown fingerprint to `drives eject`, and refuse if the identity has changed.

- model.py:230-247: same_device compares hardware_key = (serial, unique_id, model, size_bytes, bus_type).
- windows_enum.py:186: unique_id = norm_text(UniqueId), with no placeholder filtering.
- cli.py:290-296: cmd_eject selects the disk by args.disk only.

The retry then reaches _verify_mp4 (engine.py:654: detail = json.loads(it['detail'])) and adds only source_content/content. ManifestBuilder._derivatives, _raw_derivatives, _motion and html() read start_utc, end_utc and flags from that detail, so they get None or [].

Pressing Export again on the same drive gives COMPLETE. In Export_Manifest.json that video has start_utc=None, end_utc=None, start_local=None and flags=[]. Export_Summary.html shows a row with empty Starts/Ends and length '0 s'. Any 'ends abruptly', 'contains a pause' or 'clock changed' note is gone, and the video gets no motion marks. The reviewer's summary is wrong for that video.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this one, and I reproduced it end to end. In engine.py:670, _mp4_fail calls set_item_state(I_FAILED, detail=detail), and ledger.py:329-333 writes that dict as the whole detail column. The planner's {flags, start_utc, end_utc} (planner.py:327) is replaced by the failure dict. reset_failed_items (ledger.py:351) clears only state, error and sha256, so the failure dict is still there.

So _copy_phase_item goes to _existing and then _verify_mp4(existing=True). known_verified_on_drive returns None because the file was never verified. With ref_sha None the full picture check runs and passes, since the bytes on the drive are fine. Line 654 then rebuilds detail from the failure dict and adds only content and source_content. If the file had been rebuilt instead, the result would be the same, because the detail comes from the item row either way.

The manifest reads start_utc, end_utc and flags from the item detail in _derivatives (manifest.py:259-261), _raw_derivatives and _motion (303-304, 289-290), the CSV (327) and the HTML (396-401). The trigger is a transient read-back problem: a SHA mismatch, or a decode or sample error. A persistent difference would end in E-004 conflict on retry instead. On a USB drive a transient glitch is plausible. The recordings themselves are not lost. The MP4 and the originals are verified and the per-file entries keep their segment ids, so the times can be recovered. The harm is that the reviewer's summary and manifest are wrong and misleading for evidence, which is why I agree with medium.

The fix is to merge in _mp4_fail, for example dict(json.loads(it['detail'] or '{}'), failure=detail), or to rebuild start_utc, end_utc and flags from the batch plan in _verify_mp4.

ExportLedger.deferred_mp4s (ledger.py:233-238) selects only i.state='VERIFIED', so that video is never offered again. When nothing else is pending, the next press of 'Check the video on the drive' returns NOTHING_TO_EXPORT with the reassuring message. A transient MediaError (FFmpeg killed, timeout under load) that has nothing to do with the pictures is handled the same permanent way, and update_item labels it content_check='mismatch'.

With the skew removed, verify-content again prints 'All videos on this drive have already been checked picture by picture.' (state NOTHING_TO_EXPORT). The agent, seeing the second message, gives the drive to a reviewer.

Record the outcome only in content_check ('mismatch', or 'error' for decode, tool or source problems) and leave the item VERIFIED. I tried to refute this and could not; I reproduced it. The default setting is export.content_check = "sampled" (config.py:133), and the window offers "Check the video on the drive" to administrators (drive_pages.py:551, 567), so the agent can reach this path on site.

- _verify_content (engine.py:791) calls _content_check(..., existing=False).
- Any failure inside goes to _mp4_fail (engine.py:667-675). That calls set_item_state(I_FAILED). ITEM_TRANSITIONS allows VERIFIED -> FAILED (ledger.py:83), so the item becomes FAILED. The batch stays COMPLETE.

- Failures that have nothing to do with the pictures take the same path: a decoder MediaError or timeout (engine.py:710; only a removed drive is treated as an interruption), an ffprobe failure (732), a sample that cannot be decoded (743), and a video missing from the drive (790).
