confirmed.title: Install refuses after first-run setup: the setup account's Full Control and ownership of the config folder fail the code-write check, and install never removes them
confirmed.description: Setup creates %ProgramData%\Sentinel\config with D:P(A;OICI;FA;;;<setup user>)(SY)(BA). The owner is the setup user when setup is not elevated, which matches this dev machine. preflight (winsvc/__main__.py:142) runs code_write_problems on sentinel.toml and on the config folder. codeacl.write_problems allows only SYSTEM, Administrators and TrustedInstaller, so the user's FA ACE is flagged, and so is the user as owner. I verified this read-only on the dev machine: the scan of C:\ProgramData\Sentinel\config reports 'grants access mask 0x001f01ff to S-1-5-21-...-1001' and 'is owned by S-1-5-21-..., who can change its permissions'. The install plan's own config-folder step ('icacls cfg /inheritance:r /grant:r SY BA svc BU') would not fix this either: /grant:r keeps other trustees, and there is no /setowner on that folder. The service's start-up check (_running_code_problems) checks the same paths. The same leftover ACE also stays on spool/data/logs/status, so 'winsvc status' reports 'WIDER THAN EXPECTED' where bench step 1.9 expects OK.

The service cannot be installed, so recording depends on a logged-on user and stops at logoff or reboot. Also wait as long as the recorder may legitimately take: at least SHUTDOWN_BUDGET_S, or request_shutdown-style bounded stops. With resume_policy any_drive and one drive, the copier attaches it on re-insert and copies the backlog onto it at once. The one file being copied when Return is pressed is also finished first, then transferred and deleted. The same path lets an agent who picks the wrong SSD (the one in use, never taken to the office) delete its only archive copies, because the check is file sizes only. Those copies are recorded as at 'Office archive drive 3' and deleted from SSD_1, though the office never had them. They count as archived (never copied again, no A-004). With retention on, the local originals become eligible at once (TRANSFERRED counts as off-site; they are older than keep_recent_hours), so the recordings can be deleted from the laptop and lost everywhere. Transfer and delete only copies verified at or before the drive's last 'swap' index (archive_indexes reason='swap', or the archive_swap_ready event time), and leave later copies on the drive and VERIFIED. Better still, refuse Return on a drive that has had copies verified after its last swap, or that was never swapped since its last return. Add a regression test for the swap, record, re-insert, Return sequence.

I could not refute this finding, and I reproduced it.

**Why the bug happens**
- `_return_drive()` (worker.py:789) takes every VERIFIED copy on the drive from `al.copies_on(drive_id)`. That query (ledger.py:127-134) has no time or swap-index filter.
- It then marks all of them TRANSFERRED (worker.py:807) and deletes them from the drive (worker.py:808).
- The only check is that each file's size on the drive matches the ledger. Copies added after the swap pass that check, because the copier made them.
- Neither the CLI (`__main__.py _cmd_return`) nor the worker requires that the drive was swapped and not written to since.
- Nothing stops the drive being written again. After the swapped drive is absent for two scans, `_select` clears `_swapped_drive` (worker.py:334-335). When the drive is plugged back in, `_attach` treats it as an ordinary archive drive and `step()` copies the backlog at once.
- With the default `resume_policy` "any_drive" (config.py:147), that backlog is everything recorded while the drive was at the office.

**The documented procedure triggers it**
- docs/10 "On the laptop" tells the agent to plug the SSD in (step 1), refresh the list, fill in the form, then press Return (steps 2-3). The copier starts writing within seconds of step 1.
- With one SSD, days of backlog are copied and then wrongly transferred and deleted.
- With the Sabrent single-bay flow ("Swap archive drive first and take the drive in use out"), the files recorded between that swap and Return land on SSD_1 and are wrongly transferred and deleted.
- The recommended setup of two separate drives, both inserted, is mostly safe: the copier stays on the drive in use. But nothing guarantees it.

**Consequences**
- The ledger says the office holds recordings it never received.
- The archive drive's copy of those recordings is deleted.
- TRANSFERRED counts as archived (`ARCHIVED_STATES`), so the backlog shows 0. They are never copied again and no alert is raised.
- The retention manager treats TRANSFERRED as off this computer (retention/manager.py:117-122). If retention is enabled and local storage runs low, the local originals can be deleted. The recordings are then lost everywhere.
- Retention is off by default (config.py:165), so total loss depends on configuration. Even without it, the only copy left is on the laptop while every report says those recordings are archived at the office.

**Severity: high.** The archive copy is silently destroyed and the ledger is false. It becomes critical if retention is on.

**Secondary claim (wrong SSD chosen).** This one is weaker. The admin password plus the ticked office-check box is an explicit attestation, so that part is operator error. Even so, the same missing check (was the drive swapped, and has anything been copied to it since the swap?) would catch it.

- Otherwise refuse Return when the drive has copies verified after its last swap, or was not swapped since its last return.
- Also refuse to copy new files onto a drive that was swapped and not yet returned, unless the operator cancels the swap.
- Optionally show the file count from the office checklist and require it to match.

confirmed.title: Content hashing has a fixed 3600 s timeout, but segments are now 1 hour long: 5MP content hashes time out on modest hardware, waste an hour of CPU each, and raise V-001
confirmed.description: compute_content_hash decodes and SHA-256-hashes every frame with a 3600 s subprocess timeout. The default segment is now 3600 s (config.py:62, owner change 2026-11-11). The project's own measurement (PHASE2_REPORT: 5.48 s per 10 s of 2592x1944@30 on a 20-thread host, about 0.55x real time) puts a 1-hour segment at about 33 minutes on a strong desktop. FFmpeg's framehash SHA-256 of about 225 MB/s of raw pixels is single-threaded C, so a rugged laptop at below-normal priority, competing with archive copying, plausibly needs more than 60 minutes. Each timeout raises ProbeError: integrity.py:126-130 counts an attempt, writes a content_hash_failed warning event and adds to recent_errors, so service.py:623-624 shows V-001. The same fixed limits hurt elsewhere: probe_segment's 300 s timeout makes [recording] validation='decode' fail on every 1-hour segment (5 failures, V-001 CRITICAL, never sealed). The rolling audit's hard-coded batch of 12 segments (integrity.py:45) now re-hashes 12 x 2-4 GB every 10 minutes.
confirmed.failure_scenario: On the deployment laptop each hourly 5MP segment's content hash runs at full CPU for an hour and then times out. No segment ever gets content_sha256 or a frame-hash sidecar. About once an hour the agent sees 'Error V-001: Recordings could not be verified. Contact technical support...' for 10 minutes. At each restart, segments with fewer than 3 attempts are queued again and burn another hour each.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Scale the timeouts to the media: for example, timeout = max(3600, 4 * duration_s) for content hashing, and a duration-based limit for decode validation. Do not report a timeout as a V-001 operator problem (treat it as backlog). Size the audit batch by bytes (for example about 10 GB per pass) instead of a fixed 12 segments. Measure hashing throughput on the actual laptop before deployment.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the core defect, but it only fires on hardware slower than a threshold, so the reviewer's claim that it happens on the deployment laptop is not proven.

What is certain from the code:
- compute_content_hash uses a fixed `timeout=3600.0` (videohash.py:63). The only caller, IntegrityWorker.hash_segment (recorder/integrity.py:123), passes no timeout.
- segment_seconds now defaults to 3600 (config.py:62). So the timeout equals the media duration. Any machine that hashes 5MP footage slower than real time now fails every segment.
- Each failure kills FFmpeg after a full hour of work. It bumps content_hash_attempts and writes a content_hash_failed warning (integrity.py:126-130). It also adds an entry to recent_errors, which makes service.py:623-624 set verify_problem. That raises "V-001 Recordings could not be verified", whose action tells the agent to contact support.
- After 3 attempts (MAX_HASH_ATTEMPTS) the segment is never fingerprinted. While attempts remain, a restart queues it again and burns another hour.
- This contradicts the documented design. docs/05_FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md row 29 says that when content hashing cannot keep up on a slow CPU, the backlog grows and is reported to administrators with "none to operator". With the old 5-minute segments the 3600 s timeout was 12 times the duration, so a slow machine only built a backlog. The owner's change to 1-hour segments quietly turned this into recurring operator alerts.

Measured on this dev host (i7-12700K, 20 threads, FFmpeg 9.0.1), using 30 s of 2592x1944@30 H.264:
- The exact framehash sha256 command took 16.1 s (0.54x real time). Decoding alone took 1.07 s.
- So the cost is the single-threaded SHA-256 in the framehash muxer, at about 450 MB/s. Real time at 5MP@30 needs about 227 MB/s.
- A 1-hour segment therefore takes about 32 min on a top desktop P-core. The 3600 s limit is crossed by any CPU with less than about 55% of that core's sustained single-thread speed.

Hardware and settings that plausibly cross it: Celeron/Atom/i3 rugged units, a thermally throttled U-series chip under constant load, a power-saving plan, or H.265. A typical i5/i7 U-series rugged laptop is borderline, at roughly 45-55 min. The deployment laptop's CPU is not documented anywhere (PHASE2_REPORT item 4 leaves "5MP CPU load on the deployment PC" open), so whether it actually fires there is unknown.

Mitigating facts:
- Recordings are not lost. Sealing and the file SHA-256 do not depend on this worker.
- Content hashing is not the default validation path.
- The probe_segment 300 s limit only matters for the non-default validation='decode' (decode took about 2 min per hour here). It would be slower on a laptop, but it is an opt-in setting.
- The audit batch of 12 is not a live problem: audit runs in the same thread as hashing, so it never overlaps a running hash, and about 43 GB per 10 min of hashlib reads is wasteful but bounded.

Severity is medium: no recordings are lost or corrupted, but the agent gets a misleading support alert about once an hour and a CPU core is wasted, and only on hardware below the threshold.

Fix:
- Pass a timeout scaled to the media, for example max(3600, 3 * segment duration).
- Treat TimeoutExpired as backlog or "too slow", not as an operator V-001 (do not add it to recent_errors). Show it to administrators only through the content_hash_backlog figure.
- Before deployment, run the framehash command on a 5MP sample on the actual laptop.
verdict.evidence:
Code read:
- src/sentinel/media/videohash.py:61-74: `timeout: float = 3600.0`; TimeoutExpired is re-raised as ProbeError("content hashing timed out after 3600.0s").
- src/sentinel/recorder/integrity.py:123-130: the call passes no timeout. On ProbeError it increments content_hash_attempts, adds a content_hash_failed warning event and calls recent_errors.append. MAX_HASH_ATTEMPTS=3 (line 40); start() re-queues segments that are under the attempt limit (line 78).
- src/sentinel/service.py:623-624: `if any(now - t < 600 for t, _ in integ.recent_errors): verify_problem = True`, which leads to V-001 in status.py:98-101.
- src/sentinel/config.py:62: segment_seconds default 3600.0 (owner change 2026-11-11). Line 71: validation default "packets".
- src/sentinel/platform/windows.py:131-132: BELOW_NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS.
- docs/05_FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md row 29: a slow CPU should give a backlog, "none to operator".
- docs/PHASE2_REPORT.md:51 and :92: the measurement was made on the dev host; the deployment PC is still open.

- `ffmpeg -nostdin -v error -i t5mp.ts -map 0:v:0 -an -sn -dn -fps_mode passthrough -f framehash -hash sha256 -`: real 16.133 s for 910 frames, i.e. 0.54x real time, about 32 min per 1-hour segment.

- So the cost is the single-threaded SHA-256 of raw frames (about 6.8 GB in about 15 s). A CPU with under about 55% of this core's sustained single-thread SHA throughput exceeds the 3600 s timeout on every 1-hour 5MP@30 segment.

It also adds W-001, which says 'the recorder records all the time. Recording continues', whenever the detector is unhealthy (status.py:114-115), without checking whether anything is recording. The counter is reset only when a run gets media, so a W-002 also stays through a later scheduled pause (any reason except GRACEFUL_STOP counts, including SCHEDULED_PAUSE at a motion->pause edge with 0 media). A motion run also ends with 0 media, and so counts, if keep_recording_s (minimum 10 s) runs out before the first key frame arrives on a long-GOP camera.

Recording stopped. Error W-002: Motion was detected but could not be recorded. Contact technical support', then 'W-001 ... the recorder records all the time. A single failed motion run before a weekend pause leaves a CRITICAL 'Recording stopped' alert on screen for the whole planned pause.

Record `started_for_motion = snap['seconds_since_motion'] is not None and <= keep_recording_s and detector healthy` at the loop top, and leave runs ending in SCHEDULED_PAUSE out of the count. Reset motion_record_failures when the schedule mode stops being 'motion'. In status.evaluate, show W-001's 'recording continues' wording only when `flowing`, otherwise let the outage alert lead. Alternatively, rank W-002 below the R-00x outage alert when the detector is unhealthy.

I could not refute this finding. In supervisor.py, `for_motion = self._mode_now() == "motion"` (line 171) only checks the schedule mode. It does not record why the run started. Lines 191-194 then add 1 to motion_record_failures for every 0-media run in a motion period, unless the run ended in GRACEFUL_STOP. The count goes back to zero only when a run gets media (line 192); nothing resets it when the schedule mode changes.

If the camera loses power or its cable, the motion detector (which reads the same camera) gets no frames. healthy() goes false and warming_up() is false. recording_wanted() (motion.py:214-221) then returns True through the fail-safe, so _pause_reason() returns None and a recording run starts. status.evaluate then adds W-002 at CRITICAL ("Recording stopped... Motion was detected but could not be recorded"). It also adds W-001, whose action text in alerts.py:133-134 says "Recording continues". W-001 is added whenever the detector is unhealthy and never checks `flowing`.

The alerts are sorted by severity, and Python's sort keeps equal items in their original order. W-002 is added before the R-00x outage alert, so it ranks first among the CRITICAL alerts. most_severe() uses max(), which returns the first of equal items, so the banner shows W-002.

- An anchor line (append_anchor, line 551) holds only utc, seq, hash, entry_utc and reason. Nothing in it says which chain wrote it.
- _Verifier compares every anchor with this ledger. A higher seq gives log_truncated (lines 948-954). A different hash at the same seq gives anchor_mismatch (lines 1023-1030).

- _anchor_on_drive (worker.py:1361) appends to the existing Sentinel/<camera>/INDEX/chain_heads.log, so old heads stay next to new ones.
- The camera id is usually the same (CAM01). Even per-camera logs would not help, because anchors_from globs every camera folder anyway.

- Recording, copying and the chain are not affected.
- It needs a fresh ledger with a reused, uncleared drive, or a foreign drive. No deployment step tells anyone to reset the data folder; the bench test runs on the same laptop and ledger, and step 5.6a there passes.

- Put a chain identity in every anchor: `chain=<entry_hash of seq 0>` or the ledger_instance, both in the anchor line and in the manifest's recording_log_head.

- Report legacy lines without an identity that do not match as "may come from another recording computer or an earlier installation" (exit 2), not ALTERED.
- Optionally read only Sentinel/<this camera>/INDEX/chain_heads.log.
- Document this next to the fresh-installation note in docs/07.

Even so, each removed file becomes a 'file_missing' finding, so the result is ALTERED with exit status 1. docs/07 tells the operator to run `ledger verify --check-files --expect-head …` before every evidence hand-over.

First problem at log entry 3: The recording file a.ts recorded in log entry 3 is missing.' On a deployed unit with retention enabled, every hand-over check fails.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In check_key, if the verified row/latest entry has local_deleted_utc set and a retention_deletions row with state DONE exists for the segment, do not queue the file. verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this one, and I reproduced it.

How it happens:
- `_Verifier.check_key` (ledgerchain.py:1132-1133) adds every sealed segment whose latest chained record has a sha256 to the list of files to re-hash. It never looks at `local_deleted_utc`. That field is part of the chained segment projection (line 122) and may be set once (`_SEG_SET_ONCE`, line 630).
- `check_files` (lines 1186-1187) reports `file_missing` for every queued path that does not exist.
- `RetentionManager` (retention/manager.py:197-209) writes a `retention_deletions` row, sets `segments.local_deleted_utc` inside `ledger.chained(...)`, then deletes the file.

So once retention has removed an original, `verify --check-files` reports ALTERED (exit status 1), even though the removal was legitimate and recorded in the chain.

Nothing else prevents it:
- `run()` (lines 957-965) passes the file list straight to `check_files` with no filter.
- No test covers retention together with `--check-files`.
- No doc warns that removed originals will be reported.
- Other modules already treat `local_deleted_utc IS NOT NULL` as "expected absent": recorder/integrity.py:165, recorder/recovery.py:186, archive/ledger.py. The verifier is the odd one out.

Why medium and not higher:
- Retention is OFF by default (config.py:163-164). It needs an administrator to enable it and requires the archive to be enabled.
- No recordings are lost or corrupted, and the chain itself is intact.
- The impact is a false ALTERED result in the hand-over check that docs/07_SECURITY.md:290 tells the operator to run before every evidence hand-over. On a unit with retention enabled, every hand-over check would wrongly report tampering, and an agent or the office could be misled about evidence integrity.
- The workaround is to run verify without `--check-files`, or to judge each `file_missing` against its retention record.

Fix (check_key, around line 1132):
- If `last.get("local_deleted_utc")` is set, do not queue the file, and add a count note such as "N recordings were removed from this computer after archiving (retention); check them on the archive drives".
- Using the chained `last` value is safe. An attacker who sets `local_deleted_utc` to hide a deletion would still trip `record_altered` or break the chain.
- Optionally, if the file still exists (the `retention_deletions` row is still DELETING because the delete failed), still hash it.

- ledgerchain.py:122 and 630: `local_deleted_utc` is chained and may be set once.
- retention/manager.py:197-209: chained mark, then `_delete_files`.

That records an archive_drive_removed warning and attaches the other drive.

_sync_sessions (lines 378-396) only adds self.att to `present`, and self.att is now the other drive. ArchiveLedger.sync_sessions (ledger.py lines 321-344) therefore closes the still-inserted drive's session with gone_how='removed'. The only exception is a scan where scan.unusable or scan.uncertain is set.

Such a miss can really happen on Windows. VolumeScanLocator.scan (locator.py lines 134-141) drops a volume silently when read_marker raises and _marker_exists returns False. os.path.lexists returns False on any OSError, so a volume that is briefly not ready is simply omitted. This is the transient case the earlier L6 fix was meant to absorb.

- step() returned 'copied', not 'rescan'.
- One archive_drive_removed event was written.
- att switched to drive B.
- Drive A's session was closed as 'removed' and only reopened on the next scan.

- removed_unexpectedly is cleared when the next drive is attached, so the agent sees no lasting A-003 alert. The false entry stays only in the event log.
- The retention exposure is narrow. Retention is off in the code default but on in config/sentinel.example.toml, with require_removed_drive=True. A pass runs every 60 s and only when free space is below the floor. The session is reopened about 5 s later (the archive poll_interval_s). If a pass lands in that window, it can delete local originals whose only verified copy is on a drive that never left the laptop. The copy still exists, so nothing is lost outright, but the off-site rule is broken.

The copier also moves to the other drive for no reason. That is harmless to the data.

confirmed.title: An error during reconcile on attach leaves the drive attached without reconcile, which is never retried
confirmed.description: _attach assigns self.att before calling _reconcile and _write_index('attach'). If _reconcile raises an OSError while the drive is still present (PermissionError on stat, an EIO reading a damaged .partial, a refused restore rename), _drive_error returns False and the exception is re-raised with self.att still set. Any non-OSError (a sqlite lock that outlasts the retries in mark_lost, a ValueError from parse_journal's int() in _write_index) does the same. On the next step att.drive_id == key, so _attach and _reconcile are never run again for this insertion. Missing or damaged copies are not marked LOST and keep counting as archived. Stray .partial files are not removed, and the attach index is not written. Copying simply continues.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A drive comes back after an unclean unplug with one copy missing and a damaged .partial that raises EIO when hashed. The reconcile aborts and the step errors once. From then on the worker copies new recordings to the drive. The missing copy stays VERIFIED in the ledger (no A-006, backlog does not include it), and the swap index lists a file that is not on the drive. The office check then reports PROBLEM.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Set self.att only after reconcile and the initial index succeed, or wrap the post-assignment part of _attach in try/except that sets self.att = None (so the next step re-attaches and reconciles) before re-raising. In _reconcile, catch per-file OSError for a .partial: treat it as not restorable, mark the copy LOST, and continue.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding, and I reproduced it.

**What the code does**
- `_attach` (src/sentinel/archive/worker.py:544) sets `self.att` before it calls `_reconcile` (line 555).
- The only guard is `except OSError` at line 556. It hands the error to `_drive_error` (line 1061), which returns True only if the drive's root has disappeared or the disk is full. In every other case the exception goes straight back up.
- Non-OSError exceptions are not caught at all.
- `run()` (lines 264-270) catches the exception, logs it, raises `archive_error` once, sets ATTENTION and waits for the retry backoff. It never clears `self.att`.

**What happens on the next step**
- At line 423, `self.att.drive_id == key`, so `_attach` and `_reconcile` are skipped for the rest of this insertion.
- The status goes back to COPYING or UP_TO_DATE.
- `self.att` is cleared only by `_detached` (the drive is missed by two scans), `_roll_over`, or `_do_swap`. So reconcile runs again only after the drive is unplugged and reinserted or the archive service restarts.

**Ways reconcile can fail while the drive is still present**
- `p.stat()` at line 590 catches only `FileNotFoundError`. A damaged exFAT/NTFS directory entry after an unclean unplug (Windows error 1392, `PermissionError`) escapes.
- `_read_hash` on a damaged `.partial` can raise an I/O error (EIO / CRC).
- `restore_partial`, `seal_read_only` or `mark_lost` can fail, for example with a sqlite lock that outlasts the retries.

**Consequences while the drive stays in**
- Missing copies stay VERIFIED.
- Their segments are not put back in the backlog, so they are not copied again.
- There is no A-006 alert.
- Stray `.partial` files stay on the drive.
- The 'attach' index is never written.
- The swap index (`_write_index` uses `copies_on`, which returns VERIFIED rows) lists files that are not on the drive.
- If an administrator has turned on retention (off by default), it counts these phantom VERIFIED copies once the drive has left (`retention/manager.py:116-143`). It could then delete the only local original. That path is opt-in, so I am not rating the finding critical.

**Why medium and not higher**
- It needs a drive fault or an unusual error while the drive is attached.
- It clears itself on reinsertion or a service restart.
- Return-to-service separately re-checks sizes and refuses if files are missing.
- With retention off, no recording is lost. The ledger and index overstate what is on the drive, and the operator sees no lasting warning.

**Fix**
Clear `self.att = None` if anything after line 544 fails (wrap lines 554-576 in try/except BaseException, set `self.att = None`, then re-raise), or assign `self.att` only after reconcile succeeds. In `_reconcile`, handle OSError per file: treat a `.partial` that cannot be read as not restorable, and an OSError from stat as a missing copy (`mark_lost`), then carry on with the rest.

confirmed.title: On Windows, a disk with no partition table counts as BLANK ('This drive is empty'), even though Windows cannot see what is on it
confirmed.description: When a Windows disk has no partitions, classify() returns BLANK with reason no_partition_table or no_data_partitions. On Windows that only means the disk has no partition table Windows recognises. Disks used whole by other systems also show as PartitionStyle RAW with no partitions: a whole-disk LUKS, LVM, ZFS or mdraid member, a DVR or NVR disk, or a disk whose partition table was damaged. linux_enum detects such contents through lsblk FSTYPE (KIND_WHOLE_DISK, classified as foreign); windows_enum has nothing equivalent. The module docstring says 'Uncertainty always moves a drive towards the stricter path, never towards empty'. Here unknown contents move to BLANK instead, which bypasses foreign_data_authorization. In my probe, a RAW disk under policy 'never' is still BLANK with can_prepare=True, and on the interactive command line it needs no administrator and no serial, only the typed word ERASE. The only remaining protection is the ledger: a former Sentinel drive whose table was damaged, sitting in a dock that hides serials, is not recognised either.
confirmed.failure_scenario: An external disk that held a Linux LUKS or LVM volume on the whole disk, or a recorder disk from another system, is plugged into the laptop. Get-Disk shows PartitionStyle RAW with no partitions. The Drives page says 'This drive is empty and must be set up before use.' An operator erases it, and with foreign_data_authorization = 'never' the erase is still allowed. The data on it is lost.
confirmed.suggested_fix: On Windows, treat a RAW disk whose contents are unknown as FOREIGN_DATA (reason 'unknown_contents', message 'This drive contains data this computer cannot read'), so it gets the stricter path. Optionally read the first sectors read-only (there is no elevation in the unelevated listing, so do this in the elevated helper and refuse if any signature is found). At minimum, refuse BLANK for RAW disks when foreign_data_authorization is 'never'.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding. It is real, but it is unlikely to happen on the deployed laptop.

What the code does: classify() in src/sentinel/drives/classify.py treats any disk with no non-MSR partitions as BLANK (lines 260-262). The reason is no_partition_table when partition_style is None or RAW, and no_data_partitions otherwise. The operator sees "This drive is empty and must be set up before use." _preparable() (lines 285-303) applies foreign_data_authorization only to FOREIGN_DATA. A BLANK disk therefore gets can_prepare=True, needs_admin=False and needs_serial=False under every policy, including "never".

Why Windows cannot catch it: windows_enum (lines 148-193) builds partitions only from Get-Partition rows and records Get-Disk PartitionStyle. Nothing reads the disk's first sectors or looks for a signature. A disk used whole by LUKS, an LVM physical volume or an mdraid member has no MBR or GPT, so Windows reports PartitionStyle RAW with no partitions. linux_enum does catch these through lsblk FSTYPE (KIND_WHOLE_DISK, line 134), and _scan then sends them to FOREIGN_DATA. So the same disk is BLANK on Windows and FOREIGN_DATA on Linux.

The module docstring (lines 21-24) says "Uncertainty always moves a drive towards the stricter path, never towards 'empty'". This case breaks that rule. docs/04 section 4 defines BLANK as "no partition table", so the BLANK rule is intentional for a plain RAW disk. That definition assumes a disk with no partition table holds nothing, and the Linux side already shows that is not true.

On the command line (src/sentinel/drives/cli.py lines 215-249), a BLANK disk takes the else branch. Typing ERASE is enough: no --admin flag and no serial check. The UAC prompt still appears, but the on-site agent has the administrator password, so it adds no protection here.

What limits the risk:
- Erasing is off by default (erase_enabled = false in config/sentinel.example.toml line 69). It is turned on only after the dock test.
- The default policy is admin_only. Against that default, what is lost is the serial or ERASE check, the --admin step and an honest message. The outright bypass applies only under "never".
- Sentinel's own drives are GPT, so recordings are at risk only if a Sentinel drive's partition table is damaged. It would then go unrecognised only where the ledger cannot match it either: a dock with a placeholder serial, since volume IDs are gone with the table.
- The realistic loss is non-Sentinel data on an unusual drive plugged in at the remote site.

Severity is medium: a misleading operator message and a policy bypass, with low likelihood. It is not critical, because it does not threaten Sentinel recordings in normal operation.

Suggested fix: on Windows, classify a RAW disk with no partitions as FOREIGN_DATA (reason unknown_contents, message "This drive contains data this computer cannot read..."). An alternative is to keep BLANK only when the elevated helper's read of the first and last MiB finds no known signature (LUKS, LVM2 label, mdraid, ZFS label, backup GPT header). At minimum, refuse RAW disks when the policy is "never".

confirmed.title: Rename and set-up change the drive first and write the audit record last, with nothing catching a ledger error: a 'database is locked' error leaves a renamed or set-up drive with no record, which later allows duplicate SSD_n names
confirmed.description: rename_drive runs set_label() and then _write_marker(), and only after that calls audit.add_event('drive_renamed'). db.add_event has no retry, and its busy_timeout is 5 s, so 'database is locked' happens while the recorder or the archive copier holds the write lock (as in the earlier review's M9). cmd_rename catches only RenameRefused and OSError. sqlite3.OperationalError is neither, so the agent gets a traceback while the volume label and marker already carry the new name. If the agent retries, the result is 'The drive is already called SSD_7. Nothing was changed.', so the record is never written. current_names() and next_label() then do not know the new name or number. prepare._finish has the same gap (prepare.py:375): if the 'drive_prepared' event fails after the drive was formatted and marked, the command crashes, the label number is not recorded, and the drive is not a known drive by volume or filesystem serial.
confirmed.failure_scenario: The administrator renames SSD_2 to SSD_7 while the archive copier is writing; add_event raises 'database is locked'. The drive now carries SSD_7, but no record has it. The drive goes to the office. The next new drive set up gets next_label() = SSD_7, because the highest recorded number is 6 and the renamed drive is not connected. Two drives now carry stickers and labels reading SSD_7. The tamper-evident log also misses the rename.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Write the audit event before changing the drive, as an intent record carrying the old and new name (as prepare already does with drive_prepare_authorized). Alternatively, retry add_event on 'locked', and if it still fails, undo the label and the marker. In cmd_rename and cmd_prepare, catch sqlite3.Error and print a clear message saying what was and was not changed.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this. In rename_drive (src/sentinel/drives/rename.py:115-131), the order is set_label(), then _write_marker(), then audit.add_event('drive_renamed'). If _write_marker fails with OSError, the label is put back, but nothing protects the add_event step. Ledger.add_event (db.py:703) runs a single BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction under busy_timeout=5000 (db.py:450, 489) and has no retry. cmd_rename (drives/cli.py:317-322) catches only RenameRefused and OSError. sqlite3.OperationalError is neither, so it escapes as a traceback after the volume label and SENTINEL_DRIVE.json already carry the new name.

The GUI's Rename button (gui/app/drive_pages.py:502) runs the same CLI as a subprocess and then refreshes the drive list. The agent sees a traceback, but the list shows the new name, so the rename looks done. A retry is refused at rename.py:103 with "already called SSD_7. Nothing was changed.", so the record is never written.

After that, current_names() still maps the drive's uuid to its old name, and next_label() does not count the new number. While that drive is disconnected, the next drive set up gets the same SSD_n, and another drive can also be renamed to that name. The tamper-evident log also has no entry for the rename.

prepare._finish (prepare.py:375) has the same gap. The 'drive_prepared' event is written last and outside the fail() handling. cmd_prepare (cli.py:257-264) catches only PrepareRefused and PrepareFailed. If that write fails, the drive is fully set up and marked, but its label number and identity are not recorded.

The lock is a realistic risk, not a theoretical one. The codebase expects lock waits longer than 5 s from the archive and export processes: archive/ledger.py says all its writes "are retried on 'database is locked'", export/ledger.py has retry_locked with 8 attempts, and the earlier review's M9 names this exact error. The CLI here uses a plain Ledger and gets none of those retries.

Severity is medium, not higher. It needs uncommon timing: a lock held for more than 5 s while an administrator renames or sets up a drive. No recordings are lost and no wrong disk is erased. The harm is a misleading crash after a change that did succeed, a missing audit record, and a possible duplicate SSD_n sticker name later.

Fix:
- Write a 'drive_rename_authorized' intent event, carrying the old and new names, before changing the drive. Count it in current_names() and next_label().
- Alternatively, wrap the final add_event in retry_locked.

confirmed.title: When the helper's result is missing, Sentinel reports 'Nothing was erased' (Linux: any `set -e` exit with no RESULT line, such as a udevadm settle timeout after sfdisk)
confirmed.description: prepare_drive uses `step = str(res.get('step') or 'start')`, and 'start' is in NON_DESTRUCTIVE_STEPS, so when no result exists it concludes that nothing was erased. The Linux script runs under `set -eu` and prints a RESULT line only from fail() or at the end. Any command that fails outside `|| fail` stops the script silently with that command's exit code: `udevadm settle` (commands.py:289 and 294; it returns 1 when its 120 s timeout expires), `blockdev`, or the `PART=$(...)` pipeline. parse_linux_result then returns None, and the person is told 'Drive setup could not start. Nothing was erased.' after wipefs and sfdisk have already destroyed the partition table. On Windows the same happens with exit 0 or 1 and a result file that cannot be read (an antivirus lock, for example), because _read_result swallows OSError.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Linux, slow USB enclosure: wipefs and sfdisk succeed, then `udevadm settle` times out and returns 1. Because of set -e the script exits 1 with no RESULT line. Sentinel reports 'Drive setup could not start. Nothing was erased.' and records erase_started=false in the audit log. The drive is in fact wiped.
confirmed.suggested_fix: When there is no result, or the result has no step, treat the step as 'unknown' (destructive) rather than 'start'. On Linux, add a `trap 'echo "RESULT ok=0 step=$step code=2 error=aborted"' EXIT` (cleared on success), or put `|| fail 2 ...` on the udevadm, blockdev and lsblk calls, so the step reached is always reported.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding. When the helper sends back no result, prepare.py:284 uses `str(res.get("step") or "start")`. 'start' is in NON_DESTRUCTIVE_STEPS (commands.py:55), so `erased` is False. Exit codes such as 1 or 2 do not match the 3/4/5 branches, so the code reaches line 309 and reports 'Drive setup could not start. Nothing was erased.' It also writes erase_started=false to the audit log.

On Linux the script starts with `set -eu` (commands.py:252) and prints a RESULT line only from fail() or on the last line. `udevadm settle` at commands.py:289 and 294 has no `|| fail`. It returns 1 if its timeout expires, so the script ends with no RESULT line after wipefs and sfdisk have already run. parse_linux_result then returns None.

There is a related case the reviewer did not mention. If udevadm cannot be found, the shell exits 127. LinuxPkexecRunner (prepare.py:526) treats 126/127 as pkexec dismissal, so the agent is told 'Administrator approval was not given. Nothing was erased.' after the drive has been wiped.

Nothing else stops this. The timeout path supplies its own step ('unknown'), but the normal-exit path does not.

Limits on severity:
(1) Linux is the secondary platform. The deployed laptop runs Windows.
(2) On Windows the script writes the step to the result file at every Set-Step. The failure there needs _read_result to hit an OSError or ValueError after the helper has erased, which is unlikely: Defender normally opens files with sharing that still allows reads.
(3) The drive that gets wiped is the one an administrator already authorised for erasure, and a drive holding recordings is never erasable. No recordings are lost and the wrong disk is not erased.

The harm is a false 'Nothing was erased' message and a false erase_started=false audit entry on an evidence system. The partly erased drive is not flagged with the 'must not be used until set up again' warning. A retry sets it up again, so there is a workaround. That makes it medium: a misleading message plus a wrong audit record. Its practical exposure on the deployed Windows laptop is low.

Fix:
- In prepare.py, treat a missing result, or a result with no step, as step 'unknown', which counts as destructive. Only explicit 'start' or 'verify' steps from the helper, or the runner's own elevation-cancel result, should mean nothing was erased.
- In the Linux script, add `|| fail 2 udevadm_settle_failed` to both `udevadm settle` calls, or set an EXIT trap that prints `RESULT ok=0 step=$step ...` and clear it on success.
- In LinuxPkexecRunner, map 126/127 to elevation cancelled only when stdout has no RESULT line and the step never got past 'verify'. Better still, have the script print a marker line before step=clear so the runner can tell the cases apart.

- commands.py:55: `NON_DESTRUCTIVE_STEPS = ("start", "verify")`.
- commands.py:252 `set -eu`, 284 wipefs, 288 sfdisk, then 289 `udevadm settle` with no `|| fail`, 290 PART=..., 294 `udevadm settle` with no `|| fail`, 296 the only success RESULT line.
- prepare.py:526-528: exit 126/127 is mapped to EXIT_ELEVATION_CANCELLED with step 'start'.
- prepare.py:532-535: parse_linux_result returns None when there is no RESULT line.
- prepare.py:496-501: _read_result swallows OSError and ValueError.

confirmed.title: Interrupted manifest stage can loop on E-007 forever: regenerated documents are not deterministic
confirmed.description: _document raises E-007 ('regenerated document differs from the first attempt') when a document item is still PLANNED but its file already exists, and the newly generated bytes differ from expected_sha256. The documents are not deterministic, despite the claim in the manifest.py docstring. The summary HTML and Export_Manifest.json embed current_chain_head(), which moves with every ledger event, including the export's own export_failed / export_resumed events. The manifest also embeds the drive identity, which upsert_drive refreshes on each attempt and which includes mount_point, so a new drive letter changes it. The organisation comes from the live config. After E-007 the item stays PLANNED and the FAILED batch is retried with the same result every time.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Reproduced with a TargetIO that raises an OSError just after write_new has renamed the summary HTML into place, which simulates an unplug or crash after the rename and before set_item_state(COPIED). The first run fails with E-005. Every later run of the same drive fails with E-007: 'The export stopped because of a software problem... Contact technical support'. The drive can never complete its export.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Freeze every input of the documents when manifest_generated_utc is first set: chain head, drive identity (without mount_point) and organisation, stored in the batch row. Separately, if the item is PLANNED and the existing file hashes to the item's recorded expected_sha256 (bytes from an earlier attempt), accept it as VERIFIED instead of comparing it with newly generated bytes.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding, and I reproduced it. At src/sentinel/export/engine.py:882-886, _document raises E-007 when a document item is not VERIFIED, its file already exists on the drive, and the newly generated bytes hash differently from the stored expected_sha256. The summary HTML and Export_Manifest.json are not deterministic across attempts. _write_documents (engine.py:853-860) reads current_chain_head() live, and manifest.py:343 and :432 put it into the JSON and the HTML. The chain head moves with every chained event: the export's own export_failed, export_interrupted and export_resumed events, and the recorder's segment events. The manifest also embeds the drive identity, read live from the drives table (which upsert_drive refreshes), and cfg.site.organization, read live from the config.

Checks for something that already prevents the failure:
(a) A COPIED document whose file exists is verified in the VERIFYING phase (engine.py:267-269) against its stored expected_sha256. That case is handled.
(b) A PLANNED document whose file does not exist gets a new expected hash (line 883-884). That case is handled.
(c) The broken case is a PLANNED document whose file is on the drive. Three paths lead there. First, write_new succeeds in renaming the file into place, then confirm_in_place (fileio.py:265/278) raises, for example because the drive is pulled at that moment (E-002, INTERRUPTED). Second, the process is killed or loses power between write_new and set_item_state(COPIED). Third, a document read-back mismatch at line 903 marks the item FAILED with the file on disk, and reset_failed_items turns it back into PLANNED on the retry. Neither _fail nor _execute removes final files; discard_partial only touches .partial files. So every retry regenerates the documents, hits E-007, fails again and comes back to the same state.

The message tells the agent 'software problem ... Contact technical support', which is misleading. Recordings are not lost, and two workarounds exist: delete the stale document on the drive, or complete an export on a different drive, after which resumable_batch no longer offers the old FAILED batch. That puts it at medium, not high. The trigger needs a crash or unplug in a narrow window, or a read-back mismatch on a document. Once triggered, the drive cannot finish its export.

Fix:
- Freeze the document inputs (chain head, drive identity without mount_point, organisation) in the batch row when manifest_generated_utc is first set.
- In _document, when the item is PLANNED or was reset from FAILED and the existing file hashes to the stored expected_sha256, accept it as VERIFIED before comparing with the regenerated bytes.
- If the existing file matches neither, a stale file from the same batch should be discarded and rewritten, not refused with E-007.
verdict.evidence:
Code read:
- engine.py:837-909: _write_documents and _document. Line 856 uses current_chain_head(self.ledger) live. Line 882-886 raises E-007 when the item is not VERIFIED, the file exists and the bytes differ. Line 897-898 has write_new followed by set_item_state(COPIED).
- engine.py:250-273: _execute. Documents are skipped in the copy phase (line 421-422). COPIED items are verified at line 267. Only .partial files are discarded (line 259-261).
- engine.py:164-177: a FAILED batch is resumed with reset_failed_items.
- fileio.py:230-279: write_new renames, then confirm_in_place, which can raise OSError after the rename.
- manifest.py:343 and :432: the chain head is embedded in the JSON and the HTML. manifest.py:342 and :349: organisation and drive identity in the JSON.
- ledgerchain.py:527: current_chain_head returns the latest chain entry.

R2 FAILED E-007 regenerated document differs from the first attempt: Reports/Export_Summary_..._c2c52fc9.html | Error E-007: The export stopped because of a software problem. Do not remove the drive. Contact technical support and provide diagnostic report.
R3 FAILED E-007 (same)
R4 FAILED E-007 (same)
Final document items: README_FIRST.txt VERIFIED; Reports/Export_Summary_...html PLANNED.

confirmed.title: verify-content records 'full' in the ledger before writing the proof to the drive; an interruption loses it for good
confirmed.description: _verify_content calls update_item(content_check='full', ...) for each video as soon as it is checked, but writes the Content_Verification document only after the loop (line 822). If the drive is pulled during a later video, line 794 returns at once. If the document write itself fails, lines 825-828 apply. Either way, the videos already checked are 'full' in the ledger but nothing on the drive says so. deferred_mp4s() then leaves them out, so the document is never written.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Reproduced: export with content_check=deferred, then run verify-content with the drive 'unplugged' when the Content_Verification file is written. The result is INTERRUPTED E-002. The second run says 'All videos on this drive have already been checked picture by picture.' The ledger shows content_check='full', but there is no Content_Verification file on the drive, whose manifest still says 'pictures not yet checked'.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Keep the per-video results in memory, or in a pending column, and write content_check='full' / 'mismatch' only after that batch's Content_Verification document has been written and read back. Alternatively, write one document per video before updating the ledger.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this. In `_verify_content` (src/sentinel/export/engine.py:783-812), each video's `content_check='full'` is committed to the ledger right after that video passes (line 806). The `Content_Verification_*.json` proof is written only after the loop ends (lines 813-822). Three exits leave those rows at `'full'` with no document on the drive:
- an interrupted check of a later video (line 794);
- an OSError from a later video (line 799);
- a failed document write (lines 825-828).

`deferred_mp4s` (src/sentinel/export/ledger.py:233-238) selects only rows where `COALESCE(content_check,'full') != 'full'`, so those videos are never picked up again. The next run either returns NOTHING_TO_EXPORT ("All videos on this drive have already been checked picture by picture.") or checks only the remaining videos and writes a document that leaves out the earlier ones.

Nothing else prevents this:
- There is no transaction around the loop and the document write.
- There is no "pending" state.
- The verify-content CLI has no force or all option.
- The manifests and HTML already on the drive are deliberately never rewritten (docs/branches/req-review-drive-export.md:67), so they keep saying "not yet checked".

This path runs on the deployed laptop: verify-content is reachable from the GUI (gui/app/drive_pages.py) and the launcher CLI. It also covers the default `content_check='sampled'` exports, because 'sampled' != 'full'. Pulling a USB drive during a long full-frame decode of several videos is a realistic interruption.

Why medium rather than higher: no recordings are lost or corrupted, the byte-level SHA-256 verification and the manifest on the drive are intact, and the ledger result itself is true. What is lost is the on-drive proof of the full picture check for those videos. The tool then tells the operator they are already checked while the drive still says "pictures not yet checked". The only recovery is editing the database by hand. That is a misleading message plus permanently missing evidence documentation.

Fix: keep each video's result in memory, or write it to a pending column, and commit `content_check='full'`/`'mismatch'` to the ledger only after that batch's `Content_Verification` document has been written and read back. Alternatively, write and verify the document before updating each video, or let `deferred_mp4s` also return 'full' rows that have no matching `Content_Verification` document item.
verdict.evidence:
Code read:
- src/sentinel/export/engine.py:783-834: the `update_item(content_check='full', ...)` call at 806 runs inside the loop; `_document(rel, data)` at 822 runs after it; early returns at 794, 799, 826 and 828.
- src/sentinel/export/ledger.py:233-238: `deferred_mp4s` filters with `COALESCE(i.content_check,'full') != 'full'`.

Reproduced outside the repo. I copied tests/conftest.py, harness.py and test_review_export.py to <reviewer scratch folder>\vc and added a test that:
1. exports with content_check=deferred;
2. monkeypatches `ReviewExporter._document` to raise `OSError(ENODEV)` for Content_Verification paths, then runs verify_content;
3. restores `_document` and runs verify_content again.

Output:
FIRST ExportResult(state='FAILED', code='E-005', detail='OSError: [Errno 19] The device is not connected')
SECOND ExportResult(state='NOTHING_TO_EXPORT', message='All videos on this drive have already been checked picture by picture.')

DOCS []

The finding's own run reported E-002 because it unplugged the root through FaultyIO; my patch raised an OSError while the root was still present, which gives E-005. The lost state is the same in both runs.

confirmed.title: Schedule page silently rewrites valid schedule times and dates; saving (e.g. after 'Days off') can start a future pause immediately
confirmed.description: The recorder's schedule parser (schedule.py _DATE/_TIME) accepts dates like '2026-12-24T18:00', '2026-12-24 8:00', end '2026-12-24 24:00', and times with seconds such as '07:00:00'. The Schedule page cannot read these formats and puts other values in their place without saying so. parse_date_value() falls back to QDateTime.currentDateTime() when Qt cannot parse the text (line 520), or to QDate.currentDate() (line 516). normal_time()'s regex (line 418) rejects 'HH:MM:SS', so TimeCombo.set_value() puts '00:00' in a start field (line 453) and 'Midnight' (24:00) in an end field (line 460). Separately, TimeCombo.value() returns the previously selected list entry when the typed text is not a valid time (line 467), so a typo is saved as a different time than the one shown. SchedulePage.load() fills the tables with these replaced values, the preview shows them, and the next Save writes them to the file. I checked this with the venv: parse_date_value('2026-12-24T18:00', False), parse_date_value('2026-12-24 24:00', True) and parse_date_value('2026-12-24 8:00', False) all return today's date and time. TimeCombo('07:00:00').value() returns '00:00'. TimeCombo('18:30:00', end=True).value() returns '24:00'. After typing '7pm', value() returns '07:00'.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A technician hand-writes [[schedule.dates]] action='pause', start='2026-12-24T18:00', end='2026-12-27'. The recorder accepts it. Weeks later the agent opens Schedule, adds 'Days off…' and presses Save. The holiday row was loaded as start = now, so the file now says to pause from today until 27 Dec. Recording stops at once for about six weeks and P-001 tells everyone this is planned. A weekly 'record 07:00:00-18:00:00' row is saved as 00:00-Midnight, so the planned pauses and motion periods are lost.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Parse with the same rules as schedule._datetime/_seconds (or call them), accepting 'T', single-digit hours, seconds and an end of 24:00. If a stored value cannot be shown exactly, keep the original string for that row and do not rewrite it, or refuse to save with a clear message. Never fall back to 'now' or '00:00'. In TimeCombo.value(), raise a validation error for text that is not a time instead of returning currentData().

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding. I reproduced it offscreen with the venv. The recorder's parser (schedule.py:70-71, _seconds at 118 and _datetime at 131) accepts 'T' as the separator, one-digit hours, seconds and an end time of 24:00. The GUI handles less than that.
- parse_date_value (settings_pages.py:510-520) cuts the text to 16 characters and parses it with the format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'. When that fails it falls back to QDateTime.currentDateTime() or QDate.currentDate().
- normal_time (418/421) rejects HH:MM:SS. TimeCombo.set_value then puts '00:00' in a start field (453) and 'Midnight' in an end field.
- TimeCombo.value (467) returns the item that was selected before when the typed text is not a time. The typed text stays on screen, so the field shows one time and Save stores another.

SettingsPage.save (87-107) rewrites the whole [schedule] table from these widgets. It shows no diff and asks for no confirmation. So the next Save, for example after 'Days off', writes the replaced values to the file. check_text runs parse_schedule, which does not catch this, because start = now with end = 27 Dec is a valid period. One case is caught: an end of 'YYYY-MM-DD 24:00' turns into 'now', which comes before a December start, so validation refuses with a message and nothing is written.

Why I lowered the severity from high to medium:
- The dangerous date and time forms ('T', seconds, an end of 24:00, a one-digit hour after a date) are not the documented ones. config/sentinel.example.toml and the schedule.py docstring show '2026-12-24 18:00' and '2026-12-27'. Rows written by the GUI are always in the canonical form.
- A remote agent who only uses the GUI therefore never meets the date fallback. It needs a technician who hand-wrote an accepted but undocumented form.
- The typo path can happen to the agent: typing '7pm' saves the previous time. But after Save, load() re-reads the file and shows the time actually saved, and Preview shows what will happen.

The consequence is still real when the scenario happens: a future pause becomes a pause that starts now, and recording stops without anyone being told. The fix is to parse with schedule._datetime and schedule._seconds, or to keep the original string when a value cannot be shown exactly, and never fall back to now or 00:00. For text that is not a time, value() should refuse to save with a message instead of returning the previous selection.

- settings_pages.py:510-520 parse_date_value (falls back to now / today).

confirmed.title: Self-check passes on an outdated status file: 'Check everything' says the recorder works when it is dead, and the update watch cannot detect a version that does not run
confirmed.description: _status_reader() hands run_checks the plain status.read_status, which returns (doc, problem) when the heartbeat is too old. selfcheck.run_checks (selfcheck.py:80-84) only checks whether doc is None and ignores the problem. A stale document therefore yields 'Recorder running: answering', and its old overall/camera_link values are judged as current. As administrator, check_now() then calls mark_known_good() on that result. I checked this with the venv: a status.json whose heartbeat is 3600 s old, with overall=RECORDING and camera_link=connected, gives Report.ok=True, 'Everything works.' In update mode, _update_watch_failed() goes back by itself only when 'Settings file' or 'Recorder running' failed (line 828). After an update, the old version's final STOPPED document is still there, so 'Recorder running' passes and only 'Recorder state' fails. A new version whose service starts and then dies never triggers the automatic go-back.
confirmed.failure_scenario: (a) After a power cut or a watchdog os._exit, the service does not come back, and status.json still says RECORDING. The agent presses System › Check and history › Check everything and is told 'Everything works.', and these settings are saved as last known good. (b) After an update, the new SentinelService starts (so cmd_finish passes) and then crashes in a loop before writing status. Three minutes later the window shows 'This is usually not caused by the update (camera, drive)' and stays on the broken version.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In _status_reader, return (None, problem) when read_status reports a problem, or use read_status_robust and treat any kind other than OK as 'Recorder running' failed. Also make run_checks fail 'Recorder running' whenever problem is set.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding, and I reproduced it. MainWindow._status_reader (window.py:627-632) passes the plain sentinel.status.read_status to run_checks. read_status (status.py:265-267) returns (doc, "X-001 ... Last update N s ago") when the heartbeat is too old and the document is not a terminal alert. run_checks (selfcheck.py:80-84) only fails "Recorder running" when doc is None and throws `problem` away. So it says "Recorder running: answering" and judges the stale document's overall, camera_link and last_segment as if they were current.

Nothing else catches this. check_now (window.py:640-645) calls mark_known_good on the result. The dashboard on the same window uses read_status_robust (window.py:399), so the window shows X-001 "not responding" at the same moment Check everything says "Everything works." That is a direct contradiction.

Scenario (a) holds. A power cut, a hard crash, or the watchdog's os._exit leaves a non-terminal RECORDING document behind. With the default 3600 s segments, the "Recordings being saved" limit is 5520 s, so a document up to about 1.5 h old passes. The watch passes require_saved_file=False, so there any age passes.

Scenario (b) holds too. A clean stop writes overall=STOPPED with terminal=False (service.py:309, status.py:70-71). After an update the old document stays on disk, so "Recorder running" passes and only "Recorder state" fails. _update_watch_failed (window.py:828) goes back by itself only when "Settings file" or "Recorder running" failed, so it does not go back. It shows "This is usually not caused by the update (camera, drive)" instead. The automatic go-back only happens when status.json is missing or unreadable, which is almost never true on an upgraded install. It is worse if the new version wrote a RECORDING status before it hung or died: that stale document passes every tick, and the watch reports "New version checked: the recorder works."

The settings watch is mostly unaffected, because it rolls back on any failure and a stale STOPPED document fails "Recorder state."

Severity is medium, not high. Recording itself is not affected, and there is a manual way out (System › Updates go back, and the dashboard's X-001 banner). But the agent gets a misleading "Everything works", and the automatic update rollback the docs promise does not happen.

Fix: in run_checks, fail "Recorder running" whenever `problem` is set (Check("Recorder running", False, problem)) and return before judging the document. Or have _status_reader return (None, problem) when problem is set.

confirmed.title: Automatic rollback after a settings save is triggered by unrelated persistent critical alerts, so the agent's changes are reverted again and again
confirmed.description: watch_after_change()/_watch_tick() roll back to <config>.good if three passing checks in a row do not arrive within 180 s. run_checks fails whenever any alert has severity 3 (selfcheck.py:117-119). Several critical alerts persist and have nothing to do with the settings just saved: A-006 stays CRITICAL until an administrator acknowledges it, and the same applies to A-004 (archive backlog, e.g. a drive at the office), A-002 (archive drive full) and V-001. While any of these is present, no save can pass. If <config>.good differs (it was written before the alert appeared), rollback_to_known_good() restores it, restarts the recorder (another recording gap) and shows the message 'did not work with the new settings'. Every save made since the last pass is lost too.
confirmed.failure_scenario: An unacknowledged A-006 has been present for weeks. The agent adds 'Days off' on the Schedule page (or allows erasing on Storage) and saves. Three minutes later the window restores the old settings and restarts the recorder. The days off are gone, recording continues through the leave, and every further attempt is reverted the same way.
confirmed.suggested_fix: For the post-change watch, judge only what a settings change can break: settings load, recorder running with a fresh heartbeat, a healthy state, camera video, and critical alerts that were not already present before the save (take a snapshot of the alert codes at save time). Or ignore the archive (A-*) and audit (V-*) codes. When the check fails only because of such alerts, tell the agent and keep the new settings.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding, and I reproduced it.

How it fails:
1. SettingsPage.save() (settings_pages.py:87-107) writes the new file, restarts the recorder, then calls ctx.after_change(), which is AppWindow.watch_after_change() (window.py:648).
2. _watch_tick (window.py:663-698) calls check_now(), which calls selfcheck.run_checks. It needs 3 passes in a row (WATCH_PASSES). If those do not come within 180 s (WATCH_LIMIT_S), and <config>.good exists and differs from the current file, it calls rollback_to_known_good().
3. run_checks (selfcheck.py:117-119) fails whenever any alert in the recorder's status.json has severity 3, whatever its code.
4. The recorder's status.json includes archive alerts. RecorderArchiveView.evaluate (archive/status.py:190-222) adds A-006 as CRITICAL whenever the ledger has open problems; its docstring says these "persist until acknowledged". It also adds A-004 as CRITICAL once the backlog reaches backlog_alert_hours (24 h by default, config.py:153). That happens whenever the only archive drive spends more than a day at the office. The copier's own A-002 and A-008 critical alerts are merged in as well, and status.py:99 and :105 add the recorder's V-001 and V-003 as CRITICAL.
5. While such an alert is active, no check can pass. So mark_known_good() never runs and .good keeps the settings from before the alert. Any save made by the agent therefore differs from .good, and after 3 minutes it is rolled back. The rollback restarts the recorder a second time, which means another recording gap. The agent sees the misleading message "The recorder did not work with the new settings: Not working: No critical alerts: A-006", although the recorder is recording fine.
6. After the rollback, watch_after_change() runs again. The file now equals .good, so it only shows a warning; there is no endless loop. But every later save is reverted the same way for as long as the alert lasts.

Nothing prevents this. The save path does not look at existing alerts, and the watch does not compare against alerts that were already present before the save. The update watch (_update_watch_failed, window.py:819-838) handles the same problem correctly: it only acts on "Settings file" or "Recorder running" failures. The settings watch has no such filter.

Severity: medium. Recordings are not lost, only one extra restart gap per save. But the agent's changes, such as days off or a storage change, are silently undone, with a misleading reason. The workaround is to acknowledge A-006, or to wait for the drive to return before changing settings. A non-technical agent is unlikely to know that. During an office transfer (A-004), the agent cannot change settings at all until the drive is back.

Fix:
- Take a snapshot of the critical alert codes when the save is made, and make the post-change watch ignore those codes. Or count only failures that a settings change can cause: Settings file, Recorder running, Recorder state, Camera sends video, and new critical R-, C- or S- alerts.
- If the check fails only because of alerts that were already there, keep the new settings and tell the agent which alert is blocking the check.

In those cases the left-hand state label and the status bar show an INFO 'Updating to Sentinel X: recording restarts by itself' for up to an hour, whatever the recorder is actually doing. Meanwhile the Status page (which uses self.view) shows the real 'System error', so the two disagree.
confirmed.failure_scenario: The folder swap fails, and 'update restart' runs but reports 'the recorder did not start again'. The state file remains. For the next hour the window's summary and status bar tell the agent that recording restarts by itself, while nothing is being recorded.

Alternatively, have the finisher remove (or mark finished) the state file on every exit path, and have the window ignore a state file once update_result.json is newer than it.

- line 445: the recorder did not stop (exit 1)
- line 469: the program folders could not be swapped (exit 1)
- line 483: going back failed (exit 2)

confirmed.title: The SentinelArchive service writes into the recorder's recorder.log; with two processes rotating one file on Windows, log records are lost
confirmed.description: run_archive_in_host calls setup_logging(cfg.log_path, ...), which opens a RotatingFileHandler on <log_dir>\recorder.log, the same file the recorder service writes. In detached mode the archive deliberately uses archive.log (archive/__main__.py:64), and export/__main__.py:40 says 'two processes must not rotate the same file'. On Windows, rollover renames recorder.log while the other process has it open, which fails with WinError 32. The record that triggered the rollover is dropped, and the next records retry and drop again. I reproduced this with two handlers on one file (maxBytes 2000): 99 of 300 recorder records were lost and rollover failed 99 times. The archive's stream can also end up writing into a rotated or deleted backup.
confirmed.failure_scenario: After recorder.log reaches 10 MB on an installed system (days to weeks at INFO), the recorder and archive services take turns failing to rotate. A large share of recorder log lines (camera errors, recovery, R- alerts) and archive lines are silently dropped. That is exactly the material support and diagnostics (logs/recorder.log*) rely on.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Have run_archive_in_host use the archive's own handler (archive/__main__._setup_logging, which writes archive.log), or give setup_logging a file-name parameter and pass 'archive.log'. Include archive.log in diagnostics.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding. On Windows, cmd_host (winsvc/__main__.py:381-399) runs SentinelRecorder and SentinelArchive as two separate processes, each under its own virtual account. Both call logging_setup.setup_logging(cfg.log_path, ...), at line 506 for the recorder and line 561 for the archive. That function always opens a RotatingFileHandler on <log_dir>/recorder.log with maxBytes 10 MB and backupCount 10 (logging_setup.py:50-51). Nothing gives the archive service its own file. Only the detached or launcher path (archive/__main__._setup_logging, line 64) writes archive.log, and export/__main__.py:40 states the rule that two processes must not rotate the same file.

The installer grants the archive account Modify on the log folder (archive/hosting.py:64), so both processes open recorder.log successfully. Each one rotates the file on its own while the other still has its own handle and file position. In a two-process reproduction (below), most log records from both processes were lost, and in most cases nothing was reported. Some records went to files that a later rotation deleted or overwrote, and some failed rollovers dropped the record that triggered them. The backup sequence also showed gaps (.1, .3, .5, .7 and .9 were missing).

Nothing else prevents this. handleError swallows the errors silently in a service with no stderr. Once recorder.log first reaches 10 MB, every later rotation has the same contention. So camera, recovery and copier diagnostics in logs/recorder.log*, which diagnostics.py:143 bundles, become unreliable for both services. This is worse than the reviewer's figure of "a share".

Severity stays medium. Recordings, the ledger, the hash chain and status files are not affected. The loss is diagnostic logs, which support needs at a remote site.

Fix: in run_archive_in_host, use archive/__main__._setup_logging, or a setup_logging(file_name='archive.log') parameter. That keeps it identical to detached mode. Add archive.log to diagnostics.py:143.

confirmed.title: 'update finish' reports success as soon as 'sc start' is accepted; a new service that fails during start-up is not rolled back
confirmed.description: start_recording (service path) only checks the return code of 'sc start'. StartService succeeds once the process has connected to the dispatcher (START_PENDING). Everything else runs later, inside ServiceMain: load_config, setup_logging, the code-write check, and the imports of sentinel.service / sentinel.archive.worker (for example a hidden import missing from SentinelService.exe). A failure there makes the service exit with code 2 or 4 after 'sc start' has already returned 0. cmd_finish (update/cli.py:233-237) then writes outcome 'updated', and the finisher keeps the new version. check_installed never runs SentinelService.exe. The only remaining safety net is the window's 3-minute watch, which runs only in an elevated window and only after someone dismisses a modal message box. Also, when the recorder starts but SentinelArchive fails to start, cmd_finish returns 1 and the finisher tries to move the program folder while the new recorder runs from it. Move-Item fails ('Going back failed ... Call technical support') and the services are not stopped first.
confirmed.failure_scenario: An update whose SentinelService.exe fails in run_recorder_in_host (an import error, or a code-check refusal caused by the new folder's ACL). 'sc start' returns 0, so the finisher prints 'Done.', keeps the new version and deletes the state file. The recorder service crash-loops every 60 s and nothing is recorded. If nobody clicks OK on the 'updated' message in the reopened window, nothing rolls back.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In start_recording, after 'sc start', poll each service for up to about 60 s (like ServiceControl.start). Treat STOPPED with an exit code as failure, and require RUNNING. Before cmd_finish returns non-zero, stop any service it already started, so the finisher can swap the folders back.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding. `start_recording` (apply.py:261-268) checks only the return code of `sc start`, which is 0 once StartService accepts the request and the service is START_PENDING.

Most of the start-up work happens after that, inside ServiceMain:
- `ServiceHost.service_main` reports START_PENDING (scm.py:124) and then calls `run_recorder_in_host`.
- `run_recorder_in_host` (winsvc/__main__.py:482-532) imports `sentinel.service`, runs `load_config`, `setup_logging` and the code-ACL check, and only then calls `host.report_running()`.
- Any failure there ends the service with exit 2 or 4 after `sc start` has already returned 0.

`check_installed` (apply.py:517) runs inside `Sentinel.exe`. It checks the manifest, the settings and FFmpeg, but it never runs `SentinelService.exe` and never checks ACLs. So a new build whose service host fails, for example a missing hidden import, passes `update finish`. `cmd_finish` then writes outcome 'updated', the finisher prints 'Done.' and deletes the pre-update `.previous-old` folder. The version before the update is still kept in `<app>.previous`, so going back is still possible.

The one remaining safety net is in `window.py:787-806`. `show_update_result` shows a modal message box first, and only starts the 3-minute watch (which goes back by itself) after someone clicks OK. It also needs `ctx.admin`, and the window must stay open for the 3 minutes. If the agent starts the update and walks away, or closes the window, the recorder crash-loops every 60 s with nothing recorded and nothing rolls back.

The second part of the finding is also correct. If `sc start SentinelRecorder` succeeds and `sc start SentinelArchive` fails (for example error 1053), `start_recording` returns `(False, ...)`. No service is stopped, and the loop does not stop after a failure. `cmd_finish` returns 1. The finisher's rollback branch (apply.py:474-483) then runs `Move-Item $app` while the new recorder process is running from that folder, without stopping the services first. Windows refuses to rename a folder while a program runs from it, which is why the finisher waits for such processes before the first swap. The script then shows 'Going back failed ... Call technical support', exits 2, leaves the state file in place and does not reopen the window.

I could not refute this. Every settings save calls ctx.after_change(), which is watch_after_change() (settings_pages.py:106-107). That starts a 3-minute watch in which _watch_tick runs check_now/run_checks and needs 3 passes in a row. If it does not get them within WATCH_LIMIT_S, and <config>.good exists and differs from the current file, it calls rollback_to_known_good (window.py:684-694). That puts the old settings back and restarts the recorder.

run_checks fails on any alert with severity 3 in status.json (selfcheck.py:117-119). It also fails when the overall state is not in HEALTHY. The recorder's status.json always carries the archive alerts. It also merges in the archive process's own alerts (line 214), so A-004 can still come from the archive service's old threshold.

A settings save cannot clear any of these alerts. Only the update watch (_update_watch_failed) separates problems the change caused from other problems. The settings watch does not. So while A-004 or A-006 is active, every settings change the agent makes is undone 3 minutes later. The message also wrongly says the recorder did not work with the new settings.

.good is not refreshed while the alert lasts, because check_now only marks known good on a pass. It still holds the earlier healthy settings, so the rollback condition is met. After the rollback, watch_after_change runs again. It fails again, and because .good now matches the current file it shows a second warning: "There are no earlier working settings to go back to". Severity is medium, not higher. No recordings are lost, the recorder is restarted with valid earlier settings, and nothing is erased. The harm is that changes are silently undone, the operator message is misleading, and the agent cannot change settings while an archive alert is open. That matters most in the normal "only SSD at the office for more than 24 h" case, where A-004 is critical and the agent may want to turn on retention.
